items.title: Volcano v1.16 Released: NamespaceQueue, fairshare, and a broader HyperNode ecosystem
items.summary: Volcano v1.16.0 is available . v1.16.0 introduces NamespaceQueue and the fairshare plugin. Tenants can use hierarchical queues within their own namespaces to organize quotas and queue hierarchies within administrator-authorized resource pools. Fairshare brings historical resource consumption into scheduling decisions among namespaces sharing a queue, improving fairness across teams. This release also expands the HyperNode ecosystem. Platforms using other schedulers can deploy the HyperNode controller on its own to discover topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy, then integrate that information through the HyperNode API. For inference services using Volcano, new PodGroup topology anti-affinity rules can spread instances across supernodes to reduce exposure to a shared failure domain. Scheduler performance improvements include an Unschedulable Job Cache that records why Jobs could not be scheduled and skips repeated checks until blocking conditions change. Node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups also become more efficient. The release additionally brings Kubernetes 1.36 support, load estimation for bulk Pod dispatch, DRA scoring, and accelerator and stability improvements. Highlights Scheduler Performance and Scalability : An unschedulable Job cache reduces backlog retries, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups. Namespace-local Queue Hierarchies : Tenants can manage hierarchical queues, quotas, and resource sharing within their namespaces and administrator-authorized resource pools. Long-Term Fairness with fairshare : Slurm-inspired usage decay improves fairness for tenants isolated by namespace and sharing a queue. PodGroup Topology Anti-Affinity : Required and preferred rules separate workload instances across HyperNode domains. A Broader HyperNode Ecosystem : Other schedulers can reuse topology discovery and supernode management without running the other Volcano components. Key Features 1. Scheduler performance and scalability v1.16.0 introduces the Unschedulable Job Cache to improve scheduling under large pending backlogs, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups. Unschedulable Job Cache A Job may remain Pending because its queue is full, the cluster lacks suitable resources, or no node satisfies its placement constraints. Repeating the same scheduling checks in every session adds work without changing that outcome. With a large backlog, these retries also compete with newly submitted Jobs that could run. The new UnschedulableJobCache records why a Job could not be scheduled. Plugins provide event hints that identify changes which could make the Job schedulable. Subsequent sessions skip the checks covered by the cached result until a relevant change requests a retry. This reduces redundant work and improves scheduling performance in clusters with persistent unschedulable backlogs. Key capabilities : Selective skipping : Uses rejection causes to skip enqueue checks, whole-Job evaluation, or checks for particular tasks while respecting gang requirements. Event-driven wakeups : A Node label update can wake a Job blocked by node affinity. Resource release or a Queue change can wake Jobs blocked by resources or quota. Storage and DRA events are also supported through plugin hints. Safe fallback : A Job is cached only when every rejecting plugin provides a safe hint. Other Jobs continue through normal per-session evaluation. Preserved scheduling semantics : Cached Jobs remain visible to pending demand, queue accounting, and gang requirements. Normal checks run again before placement after a wakeup. Bounded retries : A watchdog retries cached Jobs after a configurable maximum skip duration, defaulting to five minutes. The in-memory cache is cleared on scheduler restart. The feature is disabled by default. Enable it with the scheduler feature gate: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.scheduler_feature_gates="UnschedulableJobCache=true" Initial coverage includes the upstream predicates integrated by Volcano, native Resource Fit, proportion, and non-hierarchical capacity. Hierarchical capacity rejections and rejections from plugins without hint providers continue to be evaluated each session. Optional per-Job debug metrics report skips, wakeups, and watchdog expirations. Related: PRs: #5848 , #5644 Design and performance results: Unschedulable Job Cache User guide: Enable the Unschedulable Job Cache Contributor: @ JesseStutler Multiple scoring plugins can now score nodes in a shared traversal, reducing scoring overhead when several plugins are active. Node updates and queue lookups also avoid unnecessary object copying and traversal. ( #5928 , #5556 , #5506 ) Volcano will continue to improve performance and scalability. Future work will explore scheduling efficiency, cache and event processing, and status updates, guided by workload benchmarks and production feedback. 2. NamespaceQueue brings queue hierarchies to Namespaces Platforms use different tenancy models. Some assign resource pools to tenants through cluster-scoped Queues. Others use namespaces as the management boundary for teams or projects and want tenants to configure queue quotas and hierarchies within that boundary. NamespaceQueue supports this namespace-based model, aligning queue management with tenant ownership. NamespaceQueue introduces a namespaced resource with the same resource-governance concepts as Queue, including capability, deserved, guarantee , and reclaimable . Administrators authorize a namespace to attach its queue hierarchy to a cluster Queue through spec.allowedNamespaces . Tenants can then manage their own hierarchy within that boundary. This separates resource-pool authorization from day-to-day tenant queue management. Different namespaces can use the same queue names without sharing queue identity. The feature is disabled by default. The Helm switch enables the participating controller, scheduler, and admission components and selects hierarchical capacity when using the chart’s default scheduler configuration: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.namespace_queue_enable=true Create the namespace and authorized parent Queue, then the tenant queue: apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: team-a --- apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: Queue metadata: name: research spec: capability: cpu: "100" memory: "200Gi" deserved: cpu: "100" memory: "200Gi" allowedNamespaces: - team-a --- apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: NamespaceQueue metadata: name: training namespace: team-a spec: parent: cluster/research capability: cpu: "40" memory: "80Gi" deserved: cpu: "40" memory: "80Gi" reclaimable: true Grant tenant RBAC permissions for namespacequeues in the tenant’s namespace. After the NamespaceQueue reports Ready=True and Authorized=True , Jobs and PodGroups in team-a can reference it with: spec: queue: namespace/training Bare names still reference cluster Queues. cluster/ identifies a cluster Queue parent, while an unprefixed parent name identifies a NamespaceQueue in the same namespace. Initial scheduling support uses hierarchical capacity. Do not enable proportion alongside it. Related: PRs: #5590 , #5629 User guide: NamespaceQueue Design: Namespace-scoped Queues Contributor: @ gitGurugu 3. fairshare improves long-term tenant fairness Volcano traditionally organizes resource sharing and quota governance around cluster-scoped Queues, which fits deployments that assign a dedicated queue to each tenant. Other platforms use namespaces as the isolation boundary for teams or projects, with multiple tenants submitting into one Queue. These deployments need fairness within that shared queue as well as fairness across queues. Current-allocation snapshots alone do not capture resource consumption over time. If a namespace keeps submitting GPU jobs, each completed job may be replaced by another from the same namespace. A tenant arriving later can wait even though the earlier tenant has already consumed substantial compute time. Inspired by Slurm fair-share scheduling, the new fairshare plugin identifies tenants by namespace and tracks cumulative resource-seconds for each namespace within a queue. Consumption decays exponentially, with a configurable half-life that defaults to four hours. Namespaces with lower historical consumption receive earlier consideration, while old usage gradually loses influence. Fairshare complements DRF’s current-resource fairness. It influences pending-job ordering and can optionally gate enqueue admission. It does not preempt jobs that are already running. Operators can choose target queues and resource types and optionally persist usage state to a ConfigMap across scheduler restarts. Example scheduler configuration: actions: "enqueue, allocate, backfill" tiers: - plugins: - name: priority - name: gang - name: conformance - name: fairshare arguments: fairshare.targetQueues: "gpu-queue" fairshare.resourceKey: "nvidia.com/gpu" fairshare.halfLifeMinutes: "240" fairshare.enableEnqueueGate: "false" fairshare.persistState: "false" - plugins: - name: drf - name: capacity - name: predicates - name: nodeorder Put fairshare before drf so historical usage can influence comparisons before DRF decides them. Keep priority first when PriorityClass should take precedence. State persistence and enqueue gating are disabled by default. Related: Feature PR: #5161 Design: Fair Share Scheduling User guide: Fairshare Plugin Feature contributor: @ dmildh-absci 4. PodGroup topology anti-affinity Keeping each workload instance within one topology domain does not ensure that different instances use separate domains. For example, multiple inference replicas can each satisfy their own network locality constraints but still land in the same supernode. A failure in that domain could affect all instances. The group-topology-affinity plugin adds required and preferred PodGroup anti-affinity across HyperNode domains. Rules select peer PodGroups by their labels and can optionally select namespaces. They compose with networkTopology, allowing each group to stay together while different groups use separate domains. Add these entries to the existing scheduler plugin list, retaining its other actions and plugins: - name: group-topology-affinity arguments: weight: 10 - name: network-topology-aware arguments: weight: 10 With a HyperNode tree containing the supernode tier, configure each participating PodGroup as follows, changing the name for each instance: apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: PodGroup metadata: name: inference-a namespace: default labels: app: model-a spec: minMember: 2 queue: default networkTopology: mode: hard highestTierName: supernode topologyAffinity: podGroupAntiAffinity: required: - podGroupSelector: matchLabels: app: model-a topologyTierName: supernode Member Pods must use schedulerName: volcano and the scheduling.k8s.io/group-name annotation. Rules match PodGroup labels, not Pod labels. A term specifies either topologyTierName or topologyTier . Preferred rules additionally use a weight from 1 to 100. Enforcement applies to allocate . BestEffort Pods placed through backfill do not receive this isolation guarantee. SubGroup affinity and anti-affinity, cross-PodGroup affinity, and automatic relocation of running Pods are outside the implemented scope. Related: PR: #5349 Design: PodGroup Topology Affinity User guide: PodGroup Anti-Affinity Contributor: @ wangyang0616 5. Expanding the HyperNode ecosystem to more schedulers Platforms using alternative schedulers may also need to discover cluster topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy. Previously, reusing HyperNode required running Volcano’s aggregate controller manager. v1.16.0 makes the HyperNode controller independently deployable, opening its topology discovery and management capabilities to more scheduling systems. Platforms can deploy just this controller and reuse existing discovery methods, including UFM and node labels. The controller creates and updates HyperNode resources and maintains the supernode hierarchy. Other schedulers can read this information through the HyperNode API and implement topology-aware placement for their workloads, without running the Volcano scheduler or its other controllers. Standalone and integrated deployments share the discovery and reconciliation implementation, allowing future discovery methods to serve both modes. Scheduling systems can share these capabilities and contribute improvements to a common implementation. The release provides a dedicated vc-hypernode-controller-manager binary, image, and Helm Deployment. The chart supports controller-manager, standalone , and disabled modes, with integrated controller-manager mode retained as the default. To install only the HyperNode controller: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.hypernode_controller_mode=standalone \ --set custom.controller_enable=false \ --set custom.scheduler_enable=false \ --set custom.admission_enable=false Discovery continues to use custom.controller_config_override . To retain the other Volcano components, change only the HyperNode mode. When migrating an existing deployment, first select disabled and wait for the controller-manager rollout before enabling standalone , ensuring a single reconciliation owner. Related: PRs: #5137 , #5136 Design: Standalone HyperNode Controller User guide: Install the Standalone HyperNode Controller Discovery configuration: HyperNode Auto Discovery Contributor: @ wangyang0616 Other notable enhancements In addition to major features, Volcano 1.16.0 brings several key enhancements: Load-Aware Scheduling for Bulk Pod Dispatch, Queue Resource Limits per Nodegroup, More Accurate NUMA Resource Accounting, DRA and Accelerator Enhancements, HyperNode Discovery and Placement Consistency, Grove and KubeRay Adopt Multi-Level Gang Scheduling, Kubernetes Compatibility and Operations. And the release also delivers essential updates across stability, correctness, and security fixes. For a complete inventory of all improvements and detailed commit histories, please refer to the release note. Upgrade Notes Upgrade to v1.16.0 through Helm or the release manifest: helm repo add volcano-sh https://volcano-sh.github.io/helm-charts helm repo update helm upgrade volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --version 1.16.0 Update CRDs and RBAC with the components before using NamespaceQueue or the new PodGroup and Numatopology fields. NamespaceQueue and UnschedulableJobCache are disabled by default. NamespaceQueue requires hierarchical capacity, whose rejections are not cached by this cache version. Review fairshare plugin order and topology anti-affinity enforcement scope before enabling them. Rebuild custom topology plugins for HyperNodeGradientResult and review the Kubernetes 1.36 integration changes. Source builds require Go 1.26. When moving HyperNode reconciliation to the standalone controller, roll out disabled mode before standalone . The existing Volcano CRDs receive retention annotations for Helm uninstall. The new NamespaceQueue CRD does not carry that annotation in this version. Review retention and ownership before reinstalling. Acknowledgements Volcano v1.16 was made possible by the collective efforts of 65 dedicated contributors around the world. Sincere thanks to everyone who contributed features, fixes, testing, documentation, and reviews—your ongoing support continues to drive Volcano’s scheduling capabilities and stability forward! References This post introduces the main capabilities in v1.16.0. For the complete API changes, bug fixes, dependency updates, maintenance items, and full list of contributors, please refer to the release notes： Release Note Full Changelog
items.summary_html:
Volcano v1.16.0 is available . v1.16.0 introduces NamespaceQueue and the fairshare plugin. Tenants can use hierarchical queues within their own namespaces to organize quotas and queue hierarchies within administrator-authorized resource pools. Fairshare brings historical resource consumption into scheduling decisions among namespaces sharing a queue, improving fairness across teams.

This release also expands the HyperNode ecosystem. Platforms using other schedulers can deploy the HyperNode controller on its own to discover topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy, then integrate that information through the HyperNode API. For inference services using Volcano, new PodGroup topology anti-affinity rules can spread instances across supernodes to reduce exposure to a shared failure domain.

Scheduler performance improvements include an Unschedulable Job Cache that records why Jobs could not be scheduled and skips repeated checks until blocking conditions change. Node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups also become more efficient. The release additionally brings Kubernetes 1.36 support, load estimation for bulk Pod dispatch, DRA scoring, and accelerator and stability improvements.

Highlights
  • Scheduler Performance and Scalability: An unschedulable Job cache reduces backlog retries, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups.
  • Namespace-local Queue Hierarchies: Tenants can manage hierarchical queues, quotas, and resource sharing within their namespaces and administrator-authorized resource pools.
  • Long-Term Fairness with fairshare: Slurm-inspired usage decay improves fairness for tenants isolated by namespace and sharing a queue.
  • PodGroup Topology Anti-Affinity: Required and preferred rules separate workload instances across HyperNode domains.
  • A Broader HyperNode Ecosystem: Other schedulers can reuse topology discovery and supernode management without running the other Volcano components.
Key Features 1. Scheduler performance and scalability

v1.16.0 introduces the Unschedulable Job Cache to improve scheduling under large pending backlogs, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups.

Unschedulable Job Cache

A Job may remain Pending because its queue is full, the cluster lacks suitable resources, or no node satisfies its placement constraints. Repeating the same scheduling checks in every session adds work without changing that outcome. With a large backlog, these retries also compete with newly submitted Jobs that could run.

The new UnschedulableJobCache records why a Job could not be scheduled. Plugins provide event hints that identify changes which could make the Job schedulable. Subsequent sessions skip the checks covered by the cached result until a relevant change requests a retry. This reduces redundant work and improves scheduling performance in clusters with persistent unschedulable backlogs.

Key capabilities:

  • Selective skipping: Uses rejection causes to skip enqueue checks, whole-Job evaluation, or checks for particular tasks while respecting gang requirements.
  • Event-driven wakeups: A Node label update can wake a Job blocked by node affinity. Resource release or a Queue change can wake Jobs blocked by resources or quota. Storage and DRA events are also supported through plugin hints.
  • Safe fallback: A Job is cached only when every rejecting plugin provides a safe hint. Other Jobs continue through normal per-session evaluation.
  • Preserved scheduling semantics: Cached Jobs remain visible to pending demand, queue accounting, and gang requirements. Normal checks run again before placement after a wakeup.
  • Bounded retries: A watchdog retries cached Jobs after a configurable maximum skip duration, defaulting to five minutes. The in-memory cache is cleared on scheduler restart.

The feature is disabled by default. Enable it with the scheduler feature gate:

helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \
  --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \
  --set custom.scheduler_feature_gates="UnschedulableJobCache=true"

Initial coverage includes the upstream predicates integrated by Volcano, native Resource Fit, proportion, and non-hierarchical capacity. Hierarchical capacity rejections and rejections from plugins without hint providers continue to be evaluated each session. Optional per-Job debug metrics report skips, wakeups, and watchdog expirations.

Related:

  • PRs: #5848, #5644
  • Design and performance results: Unschedulable Job Cache
  • User guide: Enable the Unschedulable Job Cache
  • Contributor: @JesseStutler

Multiple scoring plugins can now score nodes in a shared traversal, reducing scoring overhead when several plugins are active. Node updates and queue lookups also avoid unnecessary object copying and traversal. (#5928, #5556, #5506)

Volcano will continue to improve performance and scalability. Future work will explore scheduling efficiency, cache and event processing, and status updates, guided by workload benchmarks and production feedback.

2. NamespaceQueue brings queue hierarchies to Namespaces

Platforms use different tenancy models. Some assign resource pools to tenants through cluster-scoped Queues. Others use namespaces as the management boundary for teams or projects and want tenants to configure queue quotas and hierarchies within that boundary. NamespaceQueue supports this namespace-based model, aligning queue management with tenant ownership.

NamespaceQueue introduces a namespaced resource with the same resource-governance concepts as Queue, including capability, deserved, guarantee, and reclaimable. Administrators authorize a namespace to attach its queue hierarchy to a cluster Queue through spec.allowedNamespaces. Tenants can then manage their own hierarchy within that boundary.

This separates resource-pool authorization from day-to-day tenant queue management. Different namespaces can use the same queue names without sharing queue identity.

The feature is disabled by default. The Helm switch enables the participating controller, scheduler, and admission components and selects hierarchical capacity when using the chart’s default scheduler configuration:

helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \
  --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \
  --set custom.namespace_queue_enable=true

Create the namespace and authorized parent Queue, then the tenant queue: 

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: Queue
metadata:
  name: research
spec:
  capability:
    cpu: "100"
    memory: "200Gi"
  deserved:
    cpu: "100"
    memory: "200Gi"
  allowedNamespaces:
  - team-a
---
apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: NamespaceQueue
metadata:
  name: training
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  parent: cluster/research
  capability:
    cpu: "40"
    memory: "80Gi"
  deserved:
    cpu: "40"
    memory: "80Gi"
  reclaimable: true

Grant tenant RBAC permissions for namespacequeues in the tenant’s namespace. After the NamespaceQueue reports Ready=True and Authorized=True, Jobs and PodGroups in team-a can reference it with:

spec:
  queue: namespace/training

Bare names still reference cluster Queues. cluster/ identifies a cluster Queue parent, while an unprefixed parent name identifies a NamespaceQueue in the same namespace. Initial scheduling support uses hierarchical capacity. Do not enable proportion alongside it.

Related:

  • PRs: #5590, #5629
  • User guide: NamespaceQueue
  • Design: Namespace-scoped Queues
  • Contributor: @gitGurugu
3. fairshare improves long-term tenant fairness

Volcano traditionally organizes resource sharing and quota governance around cluster-scoped Queues, which fits deployments that assign a dedicated queue to each tenant. Other platforms use namespaces as the isolation boundary for teams or projects, with multiple tenants submitting into one Queue. These deployments need fairness within that shared queue as well as fairness across queues.

Current-allocation snapshots alone do not capture resource consumption over time. If a namespace keeps submitting GPU jobs, each completed job may be replaced by another from the same namespace. A tenant arriving later can wait even though the earlier tenant has already consumed substantial compute time.

Inspired by Slurm fair-share scheduling, the new fairshare plugin identifies tenants by namespace and tracks cumulative resource-seconds for each namespace within a queue. Consumption decays exponentially, with a configurable half-life that defaults to four hours. Namespaces with lower historical consumption receive earlier consideration, while old usage gradually loses influence.

Fairshare complements DRF’s current-resource fairness. It influences pending-job ordering and can optionally gate enqueue admission. It does not preempt jobs that are already running. Operators can choose target queues and resource types and optionally persist usage state to a ConfigMap across scheduler restarts.

Example scheduler configuration:

actions: "enqueue, allocate, backfill"
tiers:
- plugins:
  - name: priority
  - name: gang
  - name: conformance
  - name: fairshare
    arguments:
      fairshare.targetQueues: "gpu-queue"
      fairshare.resourceKey: "nvidia.com/gpu"
      fairshare.halfLifeMinutes: "240"
      fairshare.enableEnqueueGate: "false"
      fairshare.persistState: "false"
- plugins:
  - name: drf
  - name: capacity
  - name: predicates
  - name: nodeorder

Put fairshare before drf so historical usage can influence comparisons before DRF decides them. Keep priority first when PriorityClass should take precedence. State persistence and enqueue gating are disabled by default.

Related:

  • Feature PR: #5161
  • Design: Fair Share Scheduling
  • User guide: Fairshare Plugin
  • Feature contributor: @dmildh-absci
4. PodGroup topology anti-affinity

Keeping each workload instance within one topology domain does not ensure that different instances use separate domains. For example, multiple inference replicas can each satisfy their own network locality constraints but still land in the same supernode. A failure in that domain could affect all instances.

The group-topology-affinity plugin adds required and preferred PodGroup anti-affinity across HyperNode domains. Rules select peer PodGroups by their labels and can optionally select namespaces. They compose with networkTopology, allowing each group to stay together while different groups use separate domains.

Add these entries to the existing scheduler plugin list, retaining its other actions and plugins:

- name: group-topology-affinity
  arguments:
    weight: 10
- name: network-topology-aware
  arguments:
    weight: 10

With a HyperNode tree containing the supernode tier, configure each participating PodGroup as follows, changing the name for each instance:

apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: inference-a
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: model-a
spec:
  minMember: 2
  queue: default
  networkTopology:
    mode: hard
    highestTierName: supernode
  topologyAffinity:
    podGroupAntiAffinity:
      required:
      - podGroupSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: model-a
        topologyTierName: supernode

Member Pods must use schedulerName: volcano and the scheduling.k8s.io/group-name annotation. Rules match PodGroup labels, not Pod labels. A term specifies either topologyTierName or topologyTier. Preferred rules additionally use a weight from 1 to 100.

Enforcement applies to allocate. BestEffort Pods placed through backfill do not receive this isolation guarantee. SubGroup affinity and anti-affinity, cross-PodGroup affinity, and automatic relocation of running Pods are outside the implemented scope.

Related:

  • PR: #5349
  • Design: PodGroup Topology Affinity
  • User guide: PodGroup Anti-Affinity
  • Contributor: @wangyang0616
5. Expanding the HyperNode ecosystem to more schedulers

Platforms using alternative schedulers may also need to discover cluster topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy. Previously, reusing HyperNode required running Volcano’s aggregate controller manager. v1.16.0 makes the HyperNode controller independently deployable, opening its topology discovery and management capabilities to more scheduling systems.

Platforms can deploy just this controller and reuse existing discovery methods, including UFM and node labels. The controller creates and updates HyperNode resources and maintains the supernode hierarchy. Other schedulers can read this information through the HyperNode API and implement topology-aware placement for their workloads, without running the Volcano scheduler or its other controllers.

Standalone and integrated deployments share the discovery and reconciliation implementation, allowing future discovery methods to serve both modes. Scheduling systems can share these capabilities and contribute improvements to a common implementation.

The release provides a dedicated vc-hypernode-controller-manager binary, image, and Helm Deployment. The chart supports controller-manager, standalone, and disabled modes, with integrated controller-manager mode retained as the default. To install only the HyperNode controller:

helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \
  --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \
  --set custom.hypernode_controller_mode=standalone \
  --set custom.controller_enable=false \
  --set custom.scheduler_enable=false \
  --set custom.admission_enable=false

Discovery continues to use custom.controller_config_override. To retain the other Volcano components, change only the HyperNode mode. When migrating an existing deployment, first select disabled and wait for the controller-manager rollout before enabling standalone, ensuring a single reconciliation owner.

Related:

  • PRs: #5137, #5136
  • Design: Standalone HyperNode Controller
  • User guide: Install the Standalone HyperNode Controller
  • Discovery configuration: HyperNode Auto Discovery
  • Contributor: @wangyang0616
Other notable enhancements

In addition to major features, Volcano 1.16.0 brings several key enhancements: Load-Aware Scheduling for Bulk Pod Dispatch, Queue Resource Limits per Nodegroup, More Accurate NUMA Resource Accounting, DRA and Accelerator Enhancements, HyperNode Discovery and Placement Consistency, Grove and KubeRay Adopt Multi-Level Gang Scheduling, Kubernetes Compatibility and Operations. And the release also delivers essential updates across stability, correctness, and security fixes. For a complete inventory of all improvements and detailed commit histories, please refer to the release note.

Upgrade Notes

Upgrade to v1.16.0 through Helm or the release manifest:

helm repo add volcano-sh https://volcano-sh.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm upgrade volcano volcano-sh/volcano \
  --namespace volcano-system --version 1.16.0
  • Update CRDs and RBAC with the components before using NamespaceQueue or the new PodGroup and Numatopology fields.
  • NamespaceQueue and UnschedulableJobCache are disabled by default. NamespaceQueue requires hierarchical capacity, whose rejections are not cached by this cache version.
  • Review fairshare plugin order and topology anti-affinity enforcement scope before enabling them.
  • Rebuild custom topology plugins for HyperNodeGradientResult and review the Kubernetes 1.36 integration changes. Source builds require Go 1.26.
  • When moving HyperNode reconciliation to the standalone controller, roll out disabled mode before standalone.
  • The existing Volcano CRDs receive retention annotations for Helm uninstall. The new NamespaceQueue CRD does not carry that annotation in this version. Review retention and ownership before reinstalling.
Acknowledgements

Volcano v1.16 was made possible by the collective efforts of 65 dedicated contributors around the world. Sincere thanks to everyone who contributed features, fixes, testing, documentation, and reviews—your ongoing support continues to drive Volcano’s scheduling capabilities and stability forward! 

References

This post introduces the main capabilities in v1.16.0. For the complete API changes, bug fixes, dependency updates, maintenance items, and full list of contributors, please refer to the release notes：

  • Release Note
  • Full Changelog

items.title: John Strand's 11 Core Skills: For SOC Analysts
items.summary: The cybersecurity battlefield evolves daily, with SOC analysts serving as front-line defenders. After years of training SOC teams, I’ve identified 11 core skills that separate effective defenders from the rest. Here’s the problem: we’re training analysts to look for needles in haystacks when they don’t even know what hay looks like. Too many enter SOC positions without understanding the systems they’re trying to protect. 1. Understanding Operating Systems You can’t defend what you don’t understand. Period. Master both Windows and Linux. Not just surface stuff, but really get how they work under the hood. Learn through the incident response lens:”If this system were hacked, how would I find the bad guys?” 2. Network Traffic Analysis Understand TCP/IP and how traffic actually flows (the OSI model matters less than knowing what a SYN flood, DNS tunnel, or C2 beacon looks like on the wire). Know the difference between TCP and UDP, and establish baselines for what normal traffic looks like in your environment. 3. Memory Analysis Memory forensics shows you malware that might be invisible on disk. Tools like Volatility let you examine processes, connections, and DLLs from a memory dump. This works even when attackers delete their tools or use fileless malware. It’s like catching someone with their hand in the cookie jar. 4. Log Analysis Logs are your investigative breadcrumbs. Know which ones to collect and how to make sense of them. Remember, no single log tells the whole story. You need to connect multiple data points, like a detective piecing together clues at a crime scene. 5. Endpoint Detection and Response Master your EDR solutions. Understand how they work, what they can do, and where they fall short. No EDR catches everything. You need to tune these tools, like adjusting the sights on a rifle for better accuracy. 6. Threat Hunting Don’t just sit back waiting for alerts. Get out there and hunt! Look for threats that slipped past your automated systems. Combine smart hypotheses with data analysis to find attackers living off the land, using legitimate tools for evil purposes. 7. Malware Analysis Every SOC analyst should know basic static and dynamic analysis. Look at the file without running it, then observe its behavior in a safe sandbox. Learn to spot common techniques like obfuscation and persistence. Know thy enemy, right? 8. Vulnerability Management Understand different vulnerability types and how they’re exploited. Don’t just focus on CVSS scores. Consider actual exploitability in your environment and the potential impact. A “critical” vulnerability that can’t actually be exploited in your environment isn’t critical for you. 9. Incident Response When stuff hits the fan, know what to do. Identify what happened, contain it, kick out the attackers, and recover your systems. Document everything. Not just for compliance, but so your team can learn and improve. 10. Automation and Scripting Automate the boring stuff with PowerShell, Python, or Bash. Create tools that do the repetitive work for you. This frees you up to focus on the complex problems that need human brainpower. 11. Communication and Documentation Technical skills alone won’t cut it. You need to explain complex technical stuff to different audiences. The most brilliant analysis in the world is useless if you can’t make the bosses understand why they should care. items.summary_html:
The cybersecurity battlefield evolves daily, with SOC analysts serving as front-line defenders. After years of training SOC teams, I’ve identified 11 core skills that separate effective defenders from the rest.

Here’s the problem: we’re training analysts to look for needles in haystacks when they don’t even know what hay looks like. Too many enter SOC positions without understanding the systems they’re trying to protect.

1. Understanding Operating Systems

You can’t defend what you don’t understand. Period. Master both Windows and Linux. Not just surface stuff, but really get how they work under the hood. Learn through the incident response lens:”If this system were hacked, how would I find the bad guys?”

2. Network Traffic Analysis

Understand TCP/IP and how traffic actually flows (the OSI model matters less than knowing what a SYN flood, DNS tunnel, or C2 beacon looks like on the wire). Know the difference between TCP and UDP, and establish baselines for what normal traffic looks like in your environment.

3. Memory Analysis

Memory forensics shows you malware that might be invisible on disk. Tools like Volatility let you examine processes, connections, and DLLs from a memory dump. This works even when attackers delete their tools or use fileless malware. It’s like catching someone with their hand in the cookie jar.

4. Log Analysis

Logs are your investigative breadcrumbs. Know which ones to collect and how to make sense of them. Remember, no single log tells the whole story. You need to connect multiple data points, like a detective piecing together clues at a crime scene.

5. Endpoint Detection and Response

Master your EDR solutions. Understand how they work, what they can do, and where they fall short. No EDR catches everything. You need to tune these tools, like adjusting the sights on a rifle for better accuracy.

6. Threat Hunting

Don’t just sit back waiting for alerts. Get out there and hunt! Look for threats that slipped past your automated systems. Combine smart hypotheses with data analysis to find attackers living off the land, using legitimate tools for evil purposes.

7. Malware Analysis

Every SOC analyst should know basic static and dynamic analysis. Look at the file without running it, then observe its behavior in a safe sandbox. Learn to spot common techniques like obfuscation and persistence. Know thy enemy, right?

8. Vulnerability Management

Understand different vulnerability types and how they’re exploited. Don’t just focus on CVSS scores. Consider actual exploitability in your environment and the potential impact. A “critical” vulnerability that can’t actually be exploited in your environment isn’t critical for you.

9. Incident Response

When stuff hits the fan, know what to do. Identify what happened, contain it, kick out the attackers, and recover your systems. Document everything. Not just for compliance, but so your team can learn and improve.

10. Automation and Scripting

Automate the boring stuff with PowerShell, Python, or Bash. Create tools that do the repetitive work for you. This frees you up to focus on the complex problems that need human brainpower.

11. Communication and Documentation

Technical skills alone won’t cut it. You need to explain complex technical stuff to different audiences. The most brilliant analysis in the world is useless if you can’t make the bosses understand why they should care.

Conclusion

Mastering these skills won’t happen overnight, but they’re the foundation of being an effective SOC analyst. What makes great analysts stand out isn’t just knowing individual skills but connecting dots across domains: seeing how network traffic ties to endpoint behavior, when log weirdness might point to memory-resident malware, and how vulnerabilities create openings for attackers

By building these core skills, you’ll be ready to protect your organization against even the nastiest threats out there..

items.title: OffSec Launches Free PHP2Shell Lab Following Critical Vulnerability Discovery
items.summary: New York, United States, October 28th, 2026, CyberNewswire New hands-on lab lets security practitioners explore PHP2Shell exploitation firsthand as AI-assisted research reshapes vulnerability discovery. OffSec today announced the release of a free, interactive hands-on lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play) to help security practitioners examine and defend against the critical “PHP2Shell” vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) firsthand. Developed in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and active exploits targeting core PHP engines in the wild, the lab provides penetration testers and enterprise defenders with a safe, controlled environment to study the decade-old memory corruption flaws and implement timely server mitigations. The two critical flaws sat inside PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, for more than a decade. Then researchers at Wiz, a Google-owned cloud security company, pointed AI at the code. They found the first flaw Aug. 19. The next day they used it to take over a Drupal site without a password. The day after that, it worked on WordPress. PHP disclosed the flaws Oct. 21 as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. An attacker with no login can send a series of crafted web requests to crash a server or take it over. PHP’s severity scores rate both vulnerabilities as complex to exploit, even though working attacks already existed. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends patching immediately. Attackers are moving fast. Amazon calls PHP2Shell broadly exploited in the wild. By Oct.24, researchers had confirmed attackers running commands on vulnerable honeypot servers. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Oct. 26. “PHP is one of those technologies attackers love to see,” said Keegan Bowen, principal DevOps lead at OffSec . “It has been a great attack vector over the years with many exploits and potential abuses. PHP wasn’t designed with security from the start.” OffSec, which has taught hands-on offensive security since 2006, has released a free PHP2Shell lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play). The lab gives penetration testers and other security professionals a controlled environment to explore CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 firsthand. OffSec’s blog breaks down both flaws, and its proof-of-concept exploit is available on Exploit-DB . AI and the Evolving Pace of Exploitation PHP scored both flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. To build a working attack, Wiz researchers had to chain several bugs together and tune the attack to each server’s memory. When they let AI do the grind, one researcher finished in a week what once took a top team month. Attackers can use the same AI models, so flaws once ranked too complex to matter are now fair game. “At this point, attackers are heavily leaning on AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities; the rate of CVEs is roughly double what was reported last year,” said Matt Freitas-Stavola, staff software engineer at OffSec. “LLMs don’t get tired and can easily run in the background for as long as attackers have money or compute to spare. Even now, just a hint of where an issue could arise is enough for an LLM to get a workable POC out relatively quickly.” The Effects of These Flaws Both flaws start with the same weak spot: what PHP does when a request runs out of memory or hits another fatal error. “PHP is built from C and memory management becomes increasingly challenging as the code grows,” Bowen said. “Some out-of-memory states were not handled well. In some cases, attackers can access interrupted state data before it is cleaned up. That becomes an opportunity for abuse.” That leftover state can carry into the next request on the same worker. An attacker who shapes it can run code with the web server’s privileges. The same bugs can also leak data. Wiz showed attackers could potentially read memory from the PHP process. That memory could hold passwords, session tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests or the server itself. The story is still developing. On Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that can affect fully patched servers with an unusual session setup. PHP has no fix for it yet. Researchers have also built PHP2Shell exploits that get past ASLR, a common memory defense, and more issues could surface as the flaws are studied. As research continues, new vulnerabilities, exploitation techniques, and mitigations may emerge beyond those covered here. OffSec’s Current Recommendations These steps reflect what is known at the time of publication. Check CISA and the PHP project for the latest recommendations. Patch PHP Now. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Check vendor advisories rather than relying on version numbers alone. Update the Underlying PHP Engine. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or another application does not resolve vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Rebuild affected container images, and restart PHP processes so the updated code takes effect. Apply Temporary Protections While Patching. Disable PHP session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0), which also mitigates CVE-2026-115560. On PHP 8.5, disable fatal error backtraces and restart affected workers after configuration changes. These measures reduce exposure; they do not replace patching. Investigate Potential Compromise. Review web server and PHP logs for suspicious multipart requests, memory-limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, malformed session cookies, and unexpected PHP worker restarts. Investigations should consider activity dating back to at least October 17, when exploitation attempts were first reported. Rotate potentially affected credentials, API keys, and tokens as appropriate. Understand the Exploit. Strengthen the Defense. When the next disclosure lands, someone on the team needs to judge exposure. Reading about an exploit builds awareness. Working on one hands-on builds the skill to respond. OffSec’s PHP2Shell lab helps practitioners turn technical knowledge into hands-on experience they can apply to future vulnerabilities. For a deeper look at the vulnerabilities, explore OffSec’s technical analysis . Organizations looking to build these capabilities across their security teams can explore OffSec’s workforce development programs . Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning. New hands-on lab lets security practitioners explore PHP2Shell exploitation firsthand as AI-assisted research reshapes vulnerability discovery.

Developed in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and active exploits targeting core PHP engines in the wild, the lab provides penetration testers and enterprise defenders with a safe, controlled environment to study the decade-old memory corruption flaws and implement timely server mitigations.

The two critical flaws sat inside PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, for more than a decade. Then researchers at Wiz, a Google-owned cloud security company, pointed AI at the code. 

They found the first flaw Aug. 19. The next day they used it to take over a Drupal site without a password. The day after that, it worked on WordPress.

PHP disclosed the flaws Oct. 21 as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. An attacker with no login can send a series of crafted web requests to crash a server or take it over. PHP’s severity scores rate both vulnerabilities as complex to exploit, even though working attacks already existed. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends patching immediately. 

Attackers are moving fast. Amazon calls PHP2Shell broadly exploited in the wild. By Oct.24, researchers had confirmed attackers running commands on vulnerable honeypot servers. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Oct. 26. 

“PHP is one of those technologies attackers love to see,” said Keegan Bowen, principal DevOps lead at OffSec. “It has been a great attack vector over the years with many exploits and potential abuses. PHP wasn’t designed with security from the start.”

OffSec, which has taught hands-on offensive security since 2006, has released a free PHP2Shell lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play). The lab gives penetration testers and other security professionals a controlled environment to explore CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 firsthand. OffSec’s blog breaks down both flaws, and its proof-of-concept exploit is available on Exploit-DB. 

AI and the Evolving Pace of Exploitation

PHP scored both flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. To build a working attack, Wiz researchers had to chain several bugs together and tune the attack to each server’s memory. When they let AI do the grind, one researcher finished in a week what once took a top team month. Attackers can use the same AI models, so flaws once ranked too complex to matter are now fair game. 

“At this point, attackers are heavily leaning on AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities; the rate of CVEs is roughly double what was reported last year,” said Matt Freitas-Stavola, staff software engineer at OffSec. “LLMs don’t get tired and can easily run in the background for as long as attackers have money or compute to spare. Even now, just a hint of where an issue could arise is enough for an LLM to get a workable POC out relatively quickly.”

The Effects of These Flaws

Both flaws start with the same weak spot: what PHP does when a request runs out of memory or hits another fatal error.

“PHP is built from C and memory management becomes increasingly challenging as the code grows,” Bowen said. “Some out-of-memory states were not handled well. In some cases, attackers can access interrupted state data before it is cleaned up. That becomes an opportunity for abuse.”

That leftover state can carry into the next request on the same worker. An attacker who shapes it can run code with the web server’s privileges.

The same bugs can also leak data. Wiz showed attackers could potentially read memory from the PHP process. That memory could hold passwords, session tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests or the server itself. 

The story is still developing. On Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that can affect fully patched servers with an unusual session setup. PHP has no fix for it yet. Researchers have also built PHP2Shell exploits that get past ASLR, a common memory defense, and more issues could surface as the flaws are studied. As research continues, new vulnerabilities, exploitation techniques, and mitigations may emerge beyond those covered here.

OffSec’s Current Recommendations

These steps reflect what is known at the time of publication. Check CISA and the PHP project for the latest recommendations.

  • Patch PHP Now. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Check vendor advisories rather than relying on version numbers alone.
  • Update the Underlying PHP Engine. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or another application does not resolve vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Rebuild affected container images, and restart PHP processes so the updated code takes effect.
  • Apply Temporary Protections While Patching. Disable PHP session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0), which also mitigates CVE-2026-115560. On PHP 8.5, disable fatal error backtraces and restart affected workers after configuration changes. These measures reduce exposure; they do not replace patching.
  • Investigate Potential Compromise. Review web server and PHP logs for suspicious multipart requests, memory-limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, malformed session cookies, and unexpected PHP worker restarts. Investigations should consider activity dating back to at least October 17, when exploitation attempts were first reported. Rotate potentially affected credentials, API keys, and tokens as appropriate.
Understand the Exploit. Strengthen the Defense.

When the next disclosure lands, someone on the team needs to judge exposure. Reading about an exploit builds awareness. Working on one hands-on builds the skill to respond.

items.title: AI Cloners Are Here. Are Indie Devs Cooked?
items.summary: Thank you so much to everyone who has reached out to ask if I read about the Haystack Games Controversy ( here is a link to one article ) and then Drunken Goddess Reflux ( here is a link to an article about it ). You are probably here because I sent you a link after you asked me “Are we cooked?” No we are not cooked. Wait what are you talking about? In short, a developer named Nas tweeted a video of a high level prototype of their game about finding a single needle in a stack of 5 million pieces of hay. The post went viral and within a week of that viral post, the developer had a Steam page live for Needle In A Haystack Simulator. Unfortunately some other developers also created Steam pages for clone versions of that game. One of the clones actually got a demo out and another released a full version of the game before the original developer could. If you have spent any time in game dev Discords, YouTube channels, or sub-reddits, this AI cloning thing has absolutely spooked game devs. It is a controversy that combines AI AND someone stealing your game idea AND over-saturation ! It is like someone in a lab took every indie anxiety and distilled it into a serum and injected into a developer’s brain stem the moment they installed Godot 4.7.2. There is a lot of general anxiety and this is complicated so I will try to disaggregate whether we are cooked or not: TL;DR Is my game going to get cloned? – No, your game is not going to get cloned and then turned against you unless it meets ALL of these criteria: a non-bespoke art style, a fantasy that has gone EXTREMELY viral already, represents a genre that has already been explored by other games. Should I even market my game because then AI Bros will steal it? – Yes you should still market your game, and you should still do it nice and early. Should I just hide in a game dev closet and shadow drop my game so AI Bros won’t find me? – No. But if you suspect that your game is based on a quick fun “gimmick” instead of a deep experience, you should just be ready to react with a Steam page and a demo close behind just in case. But 99% of games are not this. Should I make a demo because AI Bros will decompile it and cook me? Yes you should make a demo, they are still the best way to increase visibility on your game. Should I shadow drop my game – No. This is worse than being cloned by an “AI Bro” Are indie games cooked? – No, indie games are not “cooked.” The absolute anxiety cloud hovering over the indie game industrial complex has you all looking like a bunch of sad sacks . We are video game designers here which means (other than theme park designers, candy makers, and liquor salesmen) we should be the most fun people in the world. So let me start this blog with an indie pep talk to lift up the spirits and then I will get into the data and analysis. Indie pep talk Anytime something gets really chaotic and complicated with everyone worrying about AI, crypto, saturation, bananas (etc), I find it important to do a Zack Morris Timeout and repeat my first principle about this industry: People fucking love video games to a degree that is kinda scary. Steam shoppers (specifically) spend so much money on video games because they love them, they obsess over them, spend every waking minute thinking about them, arguing over them, and actually paying for and playing them. Steam shoppers like real video games. This is their hobby and passion. Making and becoming successful in indie game development is difficult but it is not impossible because these sickos exist. The first principle of video game development (Also, I call them sickos lovingly.) Sometimes I wonder if I am being overly optimistic or ignoring something when I write these “golden age” and “don’t fear” posts. But, when I step back I have to remind myself that we are video game developers and we are working in the #1 creative medium of our era. I recently saw this chart and read this blog that compared how people spend their time in 1995 vs 2026. Look at us. “Playing a home video game” sticks out like crazy. We are winning! By a lot. Think about that! It may be hard but at least you aren’t trying to: Make movies (down 8%) Write books (down 18%) Run a sports team (down 6%) Run a bar (down 3%) I listen to podcasts and read blogs written by indie authors, film-makers, and musicians and often I hear them lament how their creative field is slowly dying. They frequently ask “how do we make our work as exciting as video games?” They blame us video game developers for the decline of films, books, and music. We are winning. We are cooking (and eating) all other creative mediums. People love, ABSOLUTELY LOVE, playing video games. The Steam playerbase is full of total sickos who buy games they will never play . The platform of Steam itself is growing every day. For the first time ever they hit 43 million concurrent players on October 11th. Steam players like our games so much they hack them to add new features. Kids spend so much time on what we make that their parents have to punish them to stop. Every backpack I see at my son’s school is Pokemon, Minecraft, Mario, or some weird character that I assume is from Roblox. Most of my kid’s friends are dressing up as video game characters for Halloween. The top Hollywood movies are based on video game IP like Minecraft (a former indie game) and Super Mario . Even indie horror game-turned-movie Iron Lung out-performed expectations . We are winning. We have cultural dominance. There is no other creative field where it is more possible for a small team to make a living directly from what they create. Can you imagine how hard it is to be a full-time writer when there are literally 250,000(!) books released every month on Amazon and readership is declining because we are becoming a post-literate society?!? Indie authors laugh at how good we have it. Yet we act like we are losers and the world is ending. We are winning so hard that, honestly, that Data for Progress chart has me a bit sad. I am a little worried games are a bit too popular. I want us all to be able to make a living doing this but … a 22% increase?!? While at the same time there is a decline in offline, tactile, in-person, human contact. Could we actually be the cigarette makers right now in this human-social health crisis? Are we the baddies ? I mean for the love of humanity, please stop doom scrolling Reddit and Youtube, maybe spend a little less time playing games, and then go read a book while on a picnic, and then ask your neighbor if they would like to come over on Halloween night and have some ghost-themed cupcakes you made (that counts as entertaining people at your home BTW!) Wait this was supposed to be a pep talk. Games are cool, at least go to a movie at a theater. That will uplift you. Boom! Pepped! Let’s go. Ironically “AI bros” are scared too All day every day I get emails and Discord DMs from developers asking “am I cooked because someone will make an AI clone of it?” But also a portion of my audience asks me “Am I cooked because I am making a game with some AI art in it. Will people yell at me and will it hurt my sales if my game is considered AI slop?” People like to blame “AI Bros” who tweet “I one-shotted GTA clone with one Fable 5 prompt. Game devs are cooked.” But for the most part, the people posting those “one shot” tweets are bros selling a product / service. But, the people making most of the “AI slop” you see in Steam Next Fest are just hobbyists who don’t yet have better game dev skills or people living in developing countries who can’t afford to hire an artist so they make do with AI. They are just not that good at making games yet and so their work looks crude. This is not to excuse AI cloning. Do not clone games. But, I just think the enemy in the AI debate is too simply depicted as an “AI-bro.” So I should say hobbyist devs who use AI to augment their skills (and may or may not be cloning or doing a fast follow) are scared too. What actually happened? I think I have read just about every article , Reddit thread, and YouTube video about the “Haystack” situation and it seems to always come down to someone saying “Haystack…. AI Slop Games…. Am-I-Rite?” and then the comment section just erupts in a doom loop about indie games while simultaneously launching into a screed against AI. Everyone is worked up into a tizzy but nobody ever took the time to look day by day at what happened. Take a breath. Time Out. Let’s disaggregate. The data comes from SteamDB for a selection of Haystack games. Needle-in-a-Haystack Games: Steam Followers Aug 22 – Oct 28, 2026 · Hover the numbered badges for what happened Switch to log scale Let me give you some more context for this timeline and those callouts. Each callout you see pertains to this list: Original tweet goes viral. Steam coming-soon pages go live for the original and two clones on the same day. The original’s developer starts running Tiktok ads but under a different name of Studio BitDot . Original paid Tiktok . Also on August 29th there was coverage by more content creators . Needle In A Haystack Simulator (Original) playtest starts. 23,000 people sign up. Notice the playtest is actually when the game gets its first wishlist spike (533 followers). The original game is way ahead of all the other clones at this point and it goes up and up from there. A playable version of the game is one of the best things you can do. Needle In A Haystack Simulator (Original) gets a publisher with Polden Publishing (well the publically set their publisher to that on that date.) The clone game Find The Needle launches a public demo (not just a playtest.) This is the first easily playable version of any of the Haystack games. It takes 13 days for the Find the Needle demo to slowly bubble through YouTube content creators. On 9/23 Orbital Potato finds the demo and you can see the velocity at which the clone Find The Needle accelerates and actually surpasses the original game in follower count on October 5th. The first full release of a Haystack clone drops on the store for sale. It has nearly the same name as the original except it is lacking the word “Simulator.” From here on out I will refer to it as Needle In A Haystack (App ID 5085740) . Note however that this game launches with a very low follower count, and its release does not slow down the momentum of the two front runners of Find The Needle and Needle In A Haystack Simulator. Clone Find The Needle takes the demo to the October Steam Next Fest. It does great and is one of the top demos of the fest. Indies are learning the wrong lessons Please reread that 2 month marketing breakdown and the follower chart above because it is much more complicated than just “AI Clones take over everything and we are cooked.” I have noticed that many of these scared indies are reacting and making decisions that run counter to what actually happened. Here are the most common incorrect reactions: “If I get cloned, I am dead, game over, I am cooked” – Not really. The original Needle In A Haystack Simulator is still growing at a healthy 60-70 followers / day. That is about 600+ wishlists / day (and that is despite not having a demo live. They should get one out there!) I estimate that the original game has about 20,000 fewer wishlists than the lead clone. That sucks but, all things considered, not that bad since they still haven’t done Steam Next Fest and they don’t have a demo. They also signed with Polden Publishing on September 1st. So they aren’t dead in the water. And look at this period of the chart when the clone released the first demo: Notice how the demo and content creator coverage was also increasing the velocity of the original game too! Also if your game does get cloned you get to reach out to the press and say “my game got cloned!” The press has a known negativity bias and they looooove to write stories about something bad happening to someone. You can ride that negativity bias to the bank. You also get to do a post on Reddit and YouTube complaining about it. So soak in the negativity (then turn it off so you can get back to work.) “I will just keep everything secret and shadow drop” – This is a sign of someone falling for the loss aversion bias . Please do not shadow drop your game ! The cloner who made Needle In A Haystack (app ID 5085740) tried to be first to market and released their game 1 month after the viral tweet. But they just did a Leroy Jenkins. They only had 452 followers at launch (estimated about 4,000 wishlists) and as you can see their following flatlined while the main 2 haystack games took off. Even AI-cloners can’t shadow drop a game and have it work. You still need to collect a lot of wishlists, do a demo, do Steam Next Fest. 6 months minimum. If you shadow drop you miss out on all the features you are paying for with your 30% Steam cut: New & Trending Free, Steam Next Fest, Personal Calendar, (hopefully) New & Trending and Popular Upcoming. Don’t surrender those because you are scared. “I am not going to make a demo because cloners will steal my game, I will just run a closed playtest” – This is a sign the developers didn’t observe what actually happened with Haystack Sim! This playtest-only approach is exactly what Needle in A Haystack Simulator did and they were still cloned and their popularity was passed when “Find The Needle” released a demo first. YouTubers like playing demos more than playtests. You must be first to market. Be brave. Don’t be a nit . Get that demo out there. “There are so many clones nobody can find any of them” – Again look at the follower chart. There really are only 3 haystack games that got more than 100 followers. Steam is good at promoting games that already have momentum and really good at hiding games with none. The first mover advantage compounds. Just try it out to see if you can find them: go to Steam and search the word “Haystack.” The number 1 game is the original. Type “needle” and the top 3 results are the top 3 games in my chart. That hasn’t changed. “AI bros just throw out slop as fast as possible and Steam players will eat it up like piggies” – Go back and read my first principle of game development. Clone #3 Needle In a Haystack (App ID 5085740) was the first to market. But it missed the mark. Something about it just isn’t as fun and it stalled out while the other 2 haystack games are still rising. I played Find The Needle (you should too in the interest of science and understanding our cloning future) and I have to admit…. it isn’t that bad. There is definitely sloppiness (there are constantly like 2 songs playing and a lot of warnings about low frame rate) but the core loop is good and interesting. YouTubers played it a lot. They are very discerning about what is fun, and they liked it. I am not condoning the cloning that Find The Needle did, but I can’t lie, the game is fun. “Marketing is cooked! We gotta throw out the playbook” – Not really. The top Haystack game used the standard indie marketing playbook . Needle In A Haystack Simulator was in the lead until the copycat put out a demo and content creators played it. You need a demo. Now the thing that has changed is maybe the speed you have to do this. I do recommend a playtest before a demo, but if you have a proven viral game, and the clones are popping up, go straight to demo. You need to make sure you are the first game that the content creators play. I also think some games are more susceptible to being cloned than others and that will change the timing of when you talk about your game and how. In my next blog I will be looking at how to determine if your game might be cloned and whether you should hold back on marketing it. Worse-case scenario I really feel bad for the original Needle In A Haystack Simulator. This is bad. But for all other indies take heart. This is like a perfect storm of events that aligned on one game: A really funny viral idea that is one of those that make you slap your head and say “why didn’t I think about that?” This is very rare. Usually I see only one or so of these a year. Past ones are Banana, Vampire Survivors, Choo Choo Charles. Unfortunately Haystack is a legendary viral idea. Find The Needle isn’t a shining example of fine craftsmanship, but it has it where it counts. And the developers didn’t just “one shot” it and slap it on Steam. This is bad, but it will likely not happen to you. That fear you are feeling is called the availability heuristic. It is this mental defect we humans have where we think something is more likely to happen based on how likely it is to come to mind. So a vivid story about the theft of a developer’s game is front of mind and every time you open Reddit there is someone doom posting about it. So it is front of mind for all of us.
