items.summary_html:
Thank you so much to everyone who has reached out to ask if I read about the Haystack Games Controversy (here is a link to one article) and then Drunken Goddess Reflux (here is a link to an article about it). You are probably here because I sent you a link after you asked me “Are we cooked?”

No we are not cooked.

Wait what are you talking about?

In short, a developer named Nas tweeted a video of a high level prototype of their game about finding a single needle in a stack of 5 million pieces of hay.

The post went viral and within a week of that viral post, the developer had a Steam page live for Needle In A Haystack Simulator. Unfortunately some other developers also created Steam pages for clone versions of that game. One of the clones actually got a demo out and another released a full version of the game before the original developer could.

If you have spent any time in game dev Discords, YouTube channels, or sub-reddits, this AI cloning thing has absolutely spooked game devs. It is a controversy that combines AI AND someone stealing your game idea AND over-saturation! It is like someone in a lab took every indie anxiety and distilled it into a serum and injected into a developer’s brain stem the moment they installed Godot 4.7.2. 

There is a lot of general anxiety and this is complicated so I will try to disaggregate whether we are cooked or not:

TL;DR

  • Is my game going to get cloned? – No, your game is not going to get cloned and then turned against you unless it meets ALL of these criteria: a non-bespoke art style, a fantasy that has gone EXTREMELY viral already, represents a genre that has already been explored by other games.
  • Should I even market my game because then AI Bros will steal it? – Yes you should still market your game, and you should still do it nice and early. 
  • Should I just hide in a game dev closet and shadow drop my game so AI Bros won’t find me? – No. But if you suspect that your game is based on a quick fun “gimmick” instead of a deep experience, you should just be ready to react with a Steam page and a demo close behind just in case. But 99% of games are not this. 
  • Should I make a demo because AI Bros will decompile it and cook me? Yes you should make a demo, they are still the best way to increase visibility on your game.
  • Should I shadow drop my game – No. This is worse than being cloned by an “AI Bro”
  • Are indie games cooked? – No, indie games are not “cooked.”

The absolute anxiety cloud hovering over the indie game industrial complex has you all looking like a bunch of sad sacks. We are video game designers here which means (other than theme park designers, candy makers, and liquor salesmen) we should be the most fun people in the world. So let me start this blog with an indie pep talk to lift up the spirits and then I will get into the data and analysis.

Indie pep talk

Anytime something gets really chaotic and complicated with everyone worrying about AI, crypto, saturation, bananas (etc), I find it important to do a Zack Morris Timeout and repeat my first principle about this industry:

People fucking love video games to a degree that is kinda scary. Steam shoppers (specifically) spend so much money on video games because they love them, they obsess over them, spend every waking minute thinking about them, arguing over them, and actually paying for and playing them. Steam shoppers like real video games. This is their hobby and passion. Making and becoming successful in indie game development is difficult but it is not impossible because these sickos exist.

The first principle of video game development (Also, I call them sickos lovingly.) 

Sometimes I wonder if I am being overly optimistic or ignoring something when I write these “golden age” and “don’t fear” posts. But, when I step back I have to remind myself that we are video game developers and we are working in the #1 creative medium of our era. 

I recently saw this chart and read this blog that compared how people spend their time in 1995 vs 2026.

Look at us. “Playing a home video game” sticks out like crazy. We are winning! By a lot. Think about that!

It may be hard but at least you aren’t trying to:

  • Make movies (down 8%)
  • Write books (down 18%)
  • Run a sports team (down 6%)
  • Run a bar (down 3%)

I listen to podcasts and read blogs written by indie authors, film-makers, and musicians and often I hear them lament how their creative field is slowly dying. They frequently ask “how do we make our work as exciting as video games?” They blame us video game developers for the decline of films, books, and music. 

We are winning. We are cooking (and eating) all other creative mediums.

People love, ABSOLUTELY LOVE, playing video games. The Steam playerbase is full of total sickos who buy games they will never play. The platform of Steam itself is growing every day. For the first time ever they hit 43 million concurrent players on October 11th.

Steam players like our games so much they hack them to add new features. Kids spend so much time on what we make that their parents have to punish them to stop. Every backpack I see at my son’s school is Pokemon, Minecraft, Mario, or some weird character that I assume is from Roblox. Most of my kid’s friends are dressing up as video game characters for Halloween. The top Hollywood movies are based on video game IP like Minecraft (a former indie game) and Super Mario. Even indie horror game-turned-movie Iron Lung out-performed expectations.

We are winning. We have cultural dominance. There is no other creative field where it is more possible for a small team to make a living directly from what they create. Can you imagine how hard it is to be a full-time writer when there are literally 250,000(!) books released every month on Amazon and readership is declining because we are becoming a post-literate society?!? Indie authors laugh at how good we have it.

Yet we act like we are losers and the world is ending. 

We are winning so hard that, honestly, that Data for Progress chart has me a bit sad. I am a little worried games are a bit too popular. I want us all to be able to make a living doing this but … a 22% increase?!? While at the same time there is a decline in offline, tactile, in-person, human contact. 

Could we actually be the cigarette makers right now in this human-social health crisis? 

Are we the baddies?

I mean for the love of humanity, please stop doom scrolling Reddit and Youtube, maybe spend a little less time playing games, and then go read a book while on a picnic, and then ask your neighbor if they would like to come over on Halloween night and have some ghost-themed cupcakes you made (that counts as entertaining people at your home BTW!)

Wait this was supposed to be a pep talk.

Games are cool, at least go to a movie at a theater.

That will uplift you.

Boom!

Pepped!

Let’s go.

Ironically “AI bros” are scared too

All day every day I get emails and Discord DMs from developers asking “am I cooked because someone will make an AI clone of it?” But also a portion of my audience asks me “Am I cooked because I am making a game with some AI art in it. Will people yell at me and will it hurt my sales if my game is considered AI slop?” 

People like to blame “AI Bros” who tweet “I one-shotted GTA clone with one Fable 5 prompt. Game devs are cooked.” But for the most part, the people posting those “one shot” tweets are bros selling a product / service. But, the people making most of the “AI slop” you see in Steam Next Fest are just hobbyists who don’t yet have better game dev skills or people living in developing countries who can’t afford to hire an artist so they make do with AI. They are just not that good at making games yet and so their work looks crude. This is not to excuse AI cloning. Do not clone games. But, I just think the enemy in the AI debate is too simply depicted as an “AI-bro.”

So I should say hobbyist devs who use AI to augment their skills (and may or may not be cloning or doing a fast follow) are scared too.

What actually happened?

I think I have read just about every article, Reddit thread, and YouTube video about the “Haystack” situation and it seems to always come down to someone saying “Haystack…. AI Slop Games…. Am-I-Rite?” and then the comment section just erupts in a doom loop about indie games while simultaneously launching into a screed against AI. 

Everyone is worked up into a tizzy but nobody ever took the time to look day by day at what happened.

Take a breath. Time Out. Let’s disaggregate. 

The data comes from SteamDB for a selection of Haystack games. 

Needle-in-a-Haystack Games: Steam Followers

Aug 22 – Oct 28, 2026 · Hover the numbered badges for what happened

Switch to log scale

Let me give you some more context for this timeline and those callouts. Each callout you see pertains to this list:

  1. Original tweet goes viral. 
  2. Steam coming-soon pages go live for the original and two clones on the same day. The original’s developer starts running Tiktok ads but under a different name of Studio BitDot. Original paid Tiktok. Also on August 29th there was coverage by more content creators. 
  3. Needle In A Haystack Simulator (Original) playtest starts. 23,000 people sign up. Notice the playtest is actually when the game gets its first wishlist spike (533 followers). The original game is way ahead of all the other clones at this point and it goes up and up from there. A playable version of the game is one of the best things you can do.
  4. Needle In A Haystack Simulator (Original) gets a publisher with Polden Publishing (well the publically set their publisher to that on that date.)
  5. The clone game Find The Needle launches a public demo (not just a playtest.) This is the first easily playable version of any of the Haystack games.
  6. It takes 13 days for the Find the Needle demo to slowly bubble through YouTube content creators. On 9/23 Orbital Potato finds the demo and you can see the velocity at which the clone Find The Needle accelerates and actually surpasses the original game in follower count on October 5th. 
  7. The first full release of a Haystack clone drops on the store for sale. It has nearly the same name as the original except it is lacking the word “Simulator.” From here on out I will refer to it as Needle In A Haystack (App ID 5085740). Note however that this game launches with a very low follower count, and its release does not slow down the momentum of the two front runners of Find The Needle and Needle In A Haystack Simulator. 
  8. Clone Find The Needle takes the demo to the October Steam Next Fest. It does great and is one of the top demos of the fest.
Indies are learning the wrong lessons

Please reread that 2 month marketing breakdown and the follower chart above because it is much more complicated than just “AI Clones take over everything and we are cooked.”

I have noticed that many of these scared indies are reacting and making decisions that run counter to what actually happened.

Here are the most common incorrect reactions:

“If I get cloned, I am dead, game over, I am cooked” – Not really. The original Needle In A Haystack Simulator is still growing at a healthy 60-70 followers / day. That is about 600+ wishlists / day (and that is despite not having a demo live. They should get one out there!) I estimate that the original game has about 20,000 fewer wishlists than the lead clone. That sucks but, all things considered, not that bad since they still haven’t done Steam Next Fest and they don’t have a demo. They also signed with Polden Publishing on September 1st. So they aren’t dead in the water. 

And look at this period of the chart when the clone released the first demo:

Notice how the demo and content creator coverage was also increasing the velocity of the original game too!

Also if your game does get cloned you get to reach out to the press and say “my game got cloned!” The press has a known negativity bias and they looooove to write stories about something bad happening to someone. You can ride that negativity bias to the bank. You also get to do a post on Reddit and YouTube complaining about it. So soak in the negativity (then turn it off so you can get back to work.)

“I will just keep everything secret and shadow drop” – This is a sign of someone falling for the loss aversion bias. Please do not shadow drop your game! The cloner who made Needle In A Haystack (app ID 5085740) tried to be first to market and released their game 1 month after the viral tweet. But they just did a Leroy Jenkins.

They only had 452 followers at launch (estimated about 4,000 wishlists) and as you can see their following flatlined while the main 2 haystack games took off. Even AI-cloners can’t shadow drop a game and have it work. You still need to collect a lot of wishlists, do a demo, do Steam Next Fest. 6 months minimum. If you shadow drop you miss out on all the features you are paying for with your 30% Steam cut: New & Trending Free, Steam Next Fest, Personal Calendar, (hopefully) New & Trending and Popular Upcoming. Don’t surrender those because you are scared.

“I am not going to make a demo because cloners will steal my game, I will just run a closed playtest” – This is a sign the developers didn’t observe what actually happened with Haystack Sim! This playtest-only approach is exactly what Needle in A Haystack Simulator did and they were still cloned and their popularity was passed when “Find The Needle” released a demo first. YouTubers like playing demos more than playtests. You must be first to market. Be brave. Don’t be a nit. Get that demo out there. 

“There are so many clones nobody can find any of them” – Again look at the follower chart. There really are only 3 haystack games that got more than 100 followers. Steam is good at promoting games that already have momentum and really good at hiding games with none. The first mover advantage compounds. Just try it out to see if you can find them: go to Steam and search the word “Haystack.” The number 1 game is the original. Type “needle” and the top 3 results are the top 3 games in my chart. If you go to Google and type “needle game” you would expect some totally vile stuff but NOPE, the original and the #1 clone are both at the top of the search results. The dozens of follow-on clones are all buried. It isn’t that hard to find the top contenders. 

This happened with the “Banana” game trend of 2024. Back then there were also so many cloned games of clickable (mostly edible) objects. But, only the first game Banana did well.

“If I release a demo the cloners can just decompile it” – Steam has a bias toward first mover advantage (with quality). With Haystack the first game and the 2 clones were the winners. The first game with a demo was the winner. The Needle In A Haystack clone that released on 9/29 didn’t do well. It wasn’t good enough. But that didn’t hurt the top ones. Your goal is to be the first to release a quality demo and a quality game. That hasn’t changed.

“AI bros just throw out slop as fast as possible and Steam players will eat it up like piggies” – Go back and read my first principle of game development. Clone #3 Needle In a Haystack (App ID 5085740) was the first to market. But it missed the mark. Something about it just isn’t as fun and it stalled out while the other 2 haystack games are still rising. I played Find The Needle (you should too in the interest of science and understanding our cloning future) and I have to admit…. it isn’t that bad. There is definitely sloppiness (there are constantly like 2 songs playing and a lot of warnings about low frame rate) but the core loop is good and interesting. YouTubers played it a lot. They are very discerning about what is fun, and they liked it. I am not condoning the cloning that Find The Needle did, but I can’t lie, the game is fun. 

“Marketing is cooked! We gotta throw out the playbook” – Not really. The top Haystack game used the standard indie marketing playbook. Get a Steam page up, get to a demo as fast as you can well before Steam Next Fest, reach out to content creators to get momentum, do Steam Next Fest. That’s the playbook and it worked great (for the cloner, and pretty good for the victim).

“AAAAAAAH!” – I think you are just stressed. Step back. Close YouTube. Close Reddit. Anytime someone posts “my game got cloned” news, look up the main game then the clone on SteamDB. Usually the clone has a fraction of the follower count and if they try to do a leroy-jenkins marketing launch they always fail. 

What has changed?

I do think getting a demo out is the best plan and that has not changed and is the cornerstone of doing well on Steam. Needle In A Haystack Simulator was in the lead until the copycat put out a demo and content creators played it. You need a demo.

Now the thing that has changed is maybe the speed you have to do this. I do recommend a playtest before a demo, but if you have a proven viral game, and the clones are popping up, go straight to demo. You need to make sure you are the first game that the content creators play. 

I also think some games are more susceptible to being cloned than others and that will change the timing of when you talk about your game and how.

In my next blog I will be looking at how to determine if your game might be cloned and whether you should hold back on marketing it. 

Worse-case scenario

I really feel bad for the original Needle In A Haystack Simulator. This is bad. But for all other indies take heart. This is like a perfect storm of events that aligned on one game:

  1. A really funny viral idea that is one of those that make you slap your head and say “why didn’t I think about that?” This is very rare. Usually I see only one or so of these a year. Past ones are Banana, Vampire Survivors, Choo Choo Charles. Unfortunately Haystack is a legendary viral idea. 
  2. Simultaneously, the idea is easy to clone because it follows core genre conventions of a very popular genre called “clean up” games. Look at this comment under the original viral tweet that accurately predicted how the game will be played:

Everyone knew the structure of this game after reading that initial tweet. That isn’t to say the game is bad, it’s just that the game design almost wrote itself. That is much easier to vibe-clone.

  1. One of the clones is actually competent. Find The Needle isn’t a shining example of fine craftsmanship, but it has it where it counts. And the developers didn’t just “one shot” it and slap it on Steam. The developers recently posted that they are on “version 8” of the demo. They are actually working on the game based on feedback like any other developer should.
  2. Needle In The Haystack Simulator (Original) is the first game to be exposed to a novel AI clone attack. At the time, we had no known natural defenses. Now we know. If you might have a viral game on your hands, proceed quietly, and get that demo ready. Move quickly but cleanly. 

Do not freak out. Do not abandon game development. This is bad, but it will likely not happen to you. 

That fear you are feeling is called the availability heuristic. It is this mental defect we humans have where we think something is more likely to happen based on how likely it is to come to mind. So a vivid story about the theft of a developer’s game is front of mind and every time you open Reddit there is someone doom posting about it. So it is front of mind for all of us. That doesn’t make it likely to happen.

It is like an airplane crash. Horrific, yes, but you are more likely to be injured on the way to the airport than on the flight itself. 

Stupid human brain. Once you can identify the availability heuristic, that should make you feel better.

Time out. Take a minute. Identify it. Get off Reddit. Get back to making your game. 

Feel better now?

items.title: Researcher Uncovers New 0-click Flaw in Telegram Stickers and Chained Them to Run Code on iOS
items.summary: Security researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says he found new zero-click bugs in Telegram stickers. He also says he chained them to run code on iOS. The work was due to be presented on October 28 at OffensiveCon in Tokyo, according to the conference agenda . Aziz says he got past Telegram’s server-side checks and that the flawed code still ships in its apps. The talk is a direct challenge to a position Telegram took in March. Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) had reported a bug in the app’s sticker code. According to reports, Telegram called the flaw fake, saying its servers check every sticker before any app can play it. ZDI then cut the severity score from 9.8 to 7.0 because of those server-side checks. The researcher behind that report, Michael DePlante, still said the weak code exists on the client side. Italy’s national cyber agency also took the report seriously. 0-click Flaw in Telegram Stickers ZDI later released its advisory ZDI-26-757 on October 15. It tracks the bug as CVE-2026-111105 and describes a numeric truncation flaw in the rlottie library. Bad input there can cause a write before the start of a memory buffer, and that can lead to code execution. The timeline shows a long back-and-forth. Telegram said on March 31 that server-side checks mitigated the bug. In mid-April, it asked ZDI for a full working exploit chain. ZDI called that request out of line with normal disclosure practice. In July, ZDI warned Telegram it would publish the case as a zero-day, which means a flaw with no patch yet. Aziz’s abstract says he spent a year on Telegram. He began by fuzzing rlottie with help from large language models. Fuzzing means feeding a program huge amounts of broken input to make it fail. The abstract says this found several memory-corruption bugs in the iOS, Android, and Desktop clients. He then found separate logic flaws in how Telegram delivers and checks stickers. By chaining them, he says he made the code that was supposed to be out of reach open to abuse. The final step was code execution on Telegram for iOS. He also plans to discuss the limits of that exploit. The public abstract gives no technical proof, no patch status, and no CVE numbers for the new bugs, so readers should treat the claims as unconfirmed until the full talk or a write-up appears. Animated stickers use the TGS format, which is a compressed Lottie animation file. Telegram’s rlottie library draws them on your screen. Pasquale Pillitteri explained that one tiny 269-byte sticker could crash Telegram and lock a chat. He also noted that server filtering does not catch every case. Telegram Desktop 7.2.7 fixed that specific variant. This is not the first time rlottie has been in trouble. A GitHub analysis recalls that Shielder found several rlottie bugs in 2021. Those affected Android, iOS, and macOS. Telegram’s code has seen other trouble lately. Cyber Security News covered a Telegram Desktop flaw tracked as CVE-2026-107181, which could let a crafted link steal files and take over accounts before version 7.2.9. We also reported on the EvilVideo bug , where fake video files ran malicious code on Android. Aziz ends his abstract with a hard question. If one provider’s servers act as the only gate against a zero-click bug, is that a fix, a design risk, or something close to a backdoor? The point is that users cannot check what the server does. They can only trust it. Until Telegram changes the client code, the safest steps are simple. Keep every Telegram app fully updated, limit who can message or add you to groups, and avoid opening files from strangers. ZDI also advises limiting interaction with the product. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

Aziz’s abstract says he spent a year on Telegram. He began by fuzzing rlottie with help from large language models. Fuzzing means feeding a program huge amounts of broken input to make it fail. The abstract says this found several memory-corruption bugs in the iOS, Android, and Desktop clients.

He then found separate logic flaws in how Telegram delivers and checks stickers. By chaining them, he says he made the code that was supposed to be out of reach open to abuse. The final step was code execution on Telegram for iOS. He also plans to discuss the limits of that exploit. The public abstract gives no technical proof, no patch status, and no CVE numbers for the new bugs, so readers should treat the claims as unconfirmed until the full talk or a write-up appears.

Animated stickers use the TGS format, which is a compressed Lottie animation file. Telegram’s rlottie library draws them on your screen. Pasquale Pillitteri explained that one tiny 269-byte sticker could crash Telegram and lock a chat. He also noted that server filtering does not catch every case. Telegram Desktop 7.2.7 fixed that specific variant.

This is not the first time rlottie has been in trouble. A GitHub analysis recalls that Shielder found several rlottie bugs in 2021. Those affected Android, iOS, and macOS.

Telegram’s code has seen other trouble lately. Cyber Security News covered a Telegram Desktop flaw tracked as CVE-2026-107181, which could let a crafted link steal files and take over accounts before version 7.2.9. We also reported on the EvilVideo bug, where fake video files ran malicious code on Android.

Aziz ends his abstract with a hard question. If one provider’s servers act as the only gate against a zero-click bug, is that a fix, a design risk, or something close to a backdoor? The point is that users cannot check what the server does. They can only trust it.

Until Telegram changes the client code, the safest steps are simple. Keep every Telegram app fully updated, limit who can message or add you to groups, and avoid opening files from strangers. ZDI also advises limiting interaction with the product.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Quickpost: Uranium Glass
items.summary: I got the opportunity to measure the radiation emitted by uranium glass . Uranium glass is glass with uranium added to the glass mix for coloration. My Bosean FS-5000 meter did not detect any radiation from the uranium glass. The counts per second (CPS) value was around the same on the uranium glass and away from it. I know it is proper uranium glass (bought at a flea market), because it glows green under ultraviolet light. My meter uses a Geiger–Müller tube , so the tube must not be sensitive enough to detect the radiation from the uranium glass. I also have another meter to measure radiation, a Radiacode 103 meter. It looks like this: It reads out a spot value of 9,57 CPS in the above picture: this is the amount of background radiation in that location, since no radioactive sources were nearby. And here is my Radiacode 103 meter inside a glass made out of uranium glass: The CPS value is 13,5, that’s noticeably higher than the background value of 9,57. Thus the glass is emitting some radiation that this meter is picking up. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t prove it’s uranium glass, because it could be another element that is the source of radiation. But this meter is not only more sensitive, it can also differentiate between sources of radiation. When my Bosean and my Radiacode meters give me a CPS value, for example 10, it means that they detected 10 ionization events per second (average). An ionization event is caused by ionization radiation: a ray or a particle. My Bosean meter uses a Geiger–Müller tube , and such a tube can only measure the presence of ionization events. It can not measure the energy of the radiation or particle. It’s a binary measure. While my Radiacode meter uses a scintillation crystal to measure ionization events. This crystal does not only detect ionization events (like a GM tube does), but it also measures the energy of the ionizing radiation that caused the ionization events. This amount of energy can be expressed in Joules, but since the values are so small, this amount is typically expressed in keV ( kiloelectonvolt ). The Radiacode meter comes with an app that can display a chart like this one: What you see here are CPS values set out per keV values. I let my meter run for 3 hours (3:02:21 exactly, see top-right corner of the image) while it was sitting inside the glass. For every ionization event, it measures the energy and builds a table of CPS per energy level. On the vertical axis, you have CPS, and on the horizontal axis, you have energy (keV). You can see a couple of peaks in this spectrum. The app has a library of spectra, and you can match that with your spectrum. That’s what I did here: the vertical purple lines come from a spectrum out of the library that I selected, and that is typical for Uranium (see top of image). The first 3 lines match a peak, the last 2 lines don’t match a peak. Here is the info displayed by the app for the Uranium chain spectrum: With the Radiacode meter, when I perform measurements over a long period, I can build up a spectrum of the energy of the ionizing radiations emitted by the sample, and then I can compare that with the app’s library, and when I have a good match, I have identified the element with a good probability. This glass that I was able to test has a very high probability of being uranium glass: it has the appearance of uranium glass, it glows under UV light, it emits radiation and its radiation spectrum matches the uranium chain spectrum. For reference, here is a spectrum of background radiation: In the EU, uranium glass can be bought and sold freely (for example at flea markets). It contains radioactive material, but it is exempt from radiation regulations. Quickpost info

items.title: Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness: Unlocking the potential of truly multi-model agentic work
items.summary: If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder. Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness , which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry . That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line. What’s a harness, and why is it hard? If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins. This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it. We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits. Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration . And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. And it had the highest satisfaction among our most demanding audience: developers. That’s why we’re standardizing all of our Copilot experiences on the strongest foundation possible. The harness is built to perform across model families , with 20+ frontier models plus bring your own key, so you can use the right model for the right job. Instead of doing the work to keep up with and eval new models, lean on us to intelligently route work to the right model or models based on the task. Our harness is flexible and configurable to any type of app, agent, or service. We recently ported the harness runtime to Rust , which has resulted in industry-leading performance and reductions in both session overhead and time-to-first token. And because the Copilot harness powers surfaces across Microsoft, it’s battle-tested and proven performant at the scale of millions of users and hundreds of real-world use cases. A unified harness lets us ship faster, learn faster, and improve Copilot over time. And because the agents you build in Foundry can run on the same harness we’ve adopted across Microsoft, our continuous harness improvements will benefit your agents, too. Try it yourself The SDK is available to download , or you can run the harness in the cloud, all managed by Foundry. Our platforms remain open and interoperable, so you can continue to bring in any harness and framework you want, too. With the Copilot harness, Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox, with governance and optimization built in from day one. You bring the instructions, skills, tools, and model choice. This is an important step towards our vision of a stronger system around the model that preserves choice. It represents the best of GitHub, brought to the Microsoft platform and beyond. We’ll keep pushing the harness forward, so you can focus on what only you can build.

TeamViewer Vulnerabilities Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code Through Remote Desktop Sessions
items.summary: TeamViewer has released security updates for three high-severity vulnerabilities that could let attackers run malicious code, crash remote desktop clients, or gain root access on macOS . The flaws affect client components used with TeamViewer Remote, TeamViewer Tensor, and TeamViewer ONE, with CVSS scores reaching 8.8. The company published security bulletin TV-2026-1011 on October 27, 2026, and urged customers to install version 15.83 or the latest available release. TeamViewer said it was not aware of active exploitation when it published the bulletin. CVE-2026-92372, rated 8.8, affects the screen-image decoder in TeamViewer Full Client for Linux and macOS before version 15.83. The decoder processes image data received during remote-control sessions. Still, it fails to check whether incoming data fits within the destination image buffer. An attacker could supply specially crafted screen-image data that writes beyond the allocated memory space, potentially allowing arbitrary code execution. A second route involves convincing a user to open a malicious TeamViewer session recording with the .tvs extension. Both routes require user interaction. TeamViewer Remote Desktop Session Flaws The bulletin also lists Linux and macOS Host installations and older 14.7 and 13.2 branches in the affected-version section. This makes it important to check installed components, not just the main desktop application. The second remote-session flaw, CVE-2026-111585, also carries an 8.8 score. It involves an integer overflow during screen processing that can lead to a heap-based buffer overflow , where data exceeds its assigned memory area. A malicious or compromised remote host could use the flaw to crash the viewer application. Depending on the platform, it could also execute code with the viewer process’s privileges. Exploitation requires the victim to establish a remote-control session with that host. Affected software includes Full Client on Windows, Linux, and macOS, Windows Portable, and the Android Remote Control app before version 15.83. CVE-2026-92374, rated 7.8, affects the privileged helper in TeamViewer Full Client and Host for macOS. It combines a timing flaw with unsafe handling of symbolic links, which point to other files or locations. A local attacker with limited permissions could exploit the gap between checking an installer package and using it. Bypassing package verification could allow installation of a malicious package and escalation to root. Unlike the screen-processing flaws, this issue requires existing local access. These fixes follow earlier reports covering TeamViewer remote-session vulnerabilities and a separate TeamViewer file-transfer vulnerability . Those reports address different flaws and should not be confused with the three newly disclosed issues in this bulletin. TeamViewer recommends updating through its official download page. items.summary_html:
TeamViewer has released security updates for three high-severity vulnerabilities that could let attackers run malicious code, crash remote desktop clients, or gain root access on macOS. The flaws affect client components used with TeamViewer Remote, TeamViewer Tensor, and TeamViewer ONE, with CVSS scores reaching 8.8.

The company published security bulletin TV-2026-1011 on October 27, 2026, and urged customers to install version 15.83 or the latest available release. TeamViewer said it was not aware of active exploitation when it published the bulletin.

CVE-2026-92372, rated 8.8, affects the screen-image decoder in TeamViewer Full Client for Linux and macOS before version 15.83. The decoder processes image data received during remote-control sessions. Still, it fails to check whether incoming data fits within the destination image buffer.

An attacker could supply specially crafted screen-image data that writes beyond the allocated memory space, potentially allowing arbitrary code execution. A second route involves convincing a user to open a malicious TeamViewer session recording with the .tvs extension. Both routes require user interaction.

TeamViewer Remote Desktop Session Flaws

The bulletin also lists Linux and macOS Host installations and older 14.7 and 13.2 branches in the affected-version section. This makes it important to check installed components, not just the main desktop application.

The second remote-session flaw, CVE-2026-111585, also carries an 8.8 score. It involves an integer overflow during screen processing that can lead to a heap-based buffer overflow, where data exceeds its assigned memory area.

A malicious or compromised remote host could use the flaw to crash the viewer application. Depending on the platform, it could also execute code with the viewer process’s privileges.

Exploitation requires the victim to establish a remote-control session with that host. Affected software includes Full Client on Windows, Linux, and macOS, Windows Portable, and the Android Remote Control app before version 15.83.

CVE-2026-92374, rated 7.8, affects the privileged helper in TeamViewer Full Client and Host for macOS. It combines a timing flaw with unsafe handling of symbolic links, which point to other files or locations.

A local attacker with limited permissions could exploit the gap between checking an installer package and using it. Bypassing package verification could allow installation of a malicious package and escalation to root. Unlike the screen-processing flaws, this issue requires existing local access.

These fixes follow earlier reports covering TeamViewer remote-session vulnerabilities and a separate TeamViewer file-transfer vulnerability. Those reports address different flaws and should not be confused with the three newly disclosed issues in this bulletin.

TeamViewer recommends updating through its official download page. Legacy fixes include 15.64.10 for Windows 7 and 8, 14.7.48868 across supported legacy platforms, and platform-specific 13.2 builds.

The key risk is that connecting to a hostile computer can expose the viewer itself. Users do not need to grant an attacker normal control of their desktop for these screen-processing vulnerabilities to become relevant.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Researchers Chain Cloudflare Security Flaws to Bypass CSP and Execute Malicious JavaScript
items.summary: Security researchers at Searchlight Cyber chained several small flaws in Cloudflare’s image feature. The chain let them run JavaScript on a site that was meant to block it. Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues published the work on October 28, 2026, in a write-up titled Cache Me If You Can . They showed a working cross-site scripting (XSS) bug through the /cdn-cgi/image/ endpoint on cloudflare.com. The write-up does not list a CVE or a patch status, so readers should check with Cloudflare. Cloudflare XSS Flaws Cloudflare sits in front of 24.3% of all websites . When a site joins Cloudflare, the company adds a managed /cdn-cgi/ path to that site’s own domain. Features such as bot checks, Web Analytics, Access, and Image Transformations live there. Because these pages load from the customer’s own domain, a bug in them runs with that site’s trust. Other researchers had already found Content Security Policy (CSP) bypasses in this path. CSP is a browser rule set that limits which scripts a page may run. Cloudflare cleans SVG images with svg-hush , a Rust tool built on the xml-rs library. The tool checks the file, then writes it back out. The researchers found that xml-rs escapes normal attribute values but writes namespace values (the xmlns setting) raw. An attacker can hide a quote mark in that value and break out of it. The filter has already approved the file by then, so the script tag slips through. Cloudflare serves these images with a strict policy of default-src ‘none’, which blocks scripts. However, the endpoint passes along Cache-Control headers from the source image. The HTTP rules allow a form such as no-cache=”Content-Security-Policy”, which tells a cache to drop the named header. Only Chromium follows this rule, and it accepts any header name. The CSP stays in place on the first load. After Chromium saves the page, the policy is gone. A known CTF trick then forces Chromium to reload the saved copy. The attacker opens the page in a new window, moves that window to another site, and calls history.back(). The opener link keeps the page out of the back/forward cache , so Chromium uses its disk cache, and the script runs. A related cache-based CSP bypass covered earlier by Cyber Security News relied on the same bfcache fallback. Image Transformations only fetches images from allowed sources. The default setting is “This zone only”. The fetcher follows redirects without checking the final address. Any open redirect on an allowed site therefore lets an attacker load an image from anywhere. The team wanted a method that needed no open redirect. They found that once Cloudflare Access is on for any hostname in a zone, /cdn-cgi/access/logout works on every hostname in that zone. Its returnTo setting accepts any cloudflare.com subdomain. A redirect on a Cloudflare research host then sent the fetcher to the attacker’s file. That completed the chain on zones with strict source settings. The team then tested the cache trick elsewhere. On Netlify Image CDN , they used it to drop both the CSP and the Content-Type header. Chromium then guessed the file type from its content and treated an SVG starting with a doctype as HTML. A processing instruction hid the script from the SVGO cleaner, which only checks elements. The researchers say Netlify’s hosted code is not public, so they could not confirm it matches the open-source version. Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage also allow signed links to override response headers. Such links can set response-content-type and response-cache-control. This matters for buckets behind custom domains or proxies that pass query strings along. The idea builds on earlier Content-Type override research and the S3 GetObject overrides . The main lesson is that you shouldn’t trust only a file’s body. Headers passed through by an image service or storage layer become part of your security. Teams should avoid forwarding Cache-Control and X-* headers from untrusted sources. They should also set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and review which sources their image tools may fetch. Closing open redirects helps too. Past work shows that even strong filters can fail, as in WAF bypass research on XSS payloads. Layered defenses still matter. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: PropellerAds: Why Modern Malware Delivery Starts Before the Payload
items.summary: By Farukh Rakhimov , Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding In March 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) disclosed Coruna, an iOS exploit kit with five exploit chains and 23 exploits covering iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1. The most instructive part of the disclosure is what happened before the exploit got any chance to run. Coruna was amazingly picky about visitors. A JavaScript fingerprinting module checked whether the visitor was a real device, which iPhone model it was and which iOS version it ran. Only then did the framework fire a matching exploit. Researchers, scanners, Lockdown Mode devices and private browsing sessions were shown the door. For a defender, the payload is where the investigation starts. For the operator, it is the end of the assembly line: by then, traffic has already been acquired, routed and qualified, mostly in plain view. At PropellerAds, we see that upstream layer from the advertising side, including through ADEX, our traffic-quality and anti-fraud system. A malware campaign is a delivery system A modern malware campaign makes a lot more sense if you look at it as a delivery system. It usually has five parts: Acquisition: a paid ad, a search result, a compromised site, a messenger link. Routing: redirectors and traffic distribution systems (TDS) that decide where each visitor goes next. Trusted infrastructure: CDNs, code repositories and file-sharing services that help malicious traffic blend into the furniture well. Visitor qualification: fingerprinting that decides who gets the payload and who gets a decoy. Persuasion: a fake download page, a fake virus alert, or a chat in WhatsApp or Telegram. In June 2026, Check Point Research described fake open-source download sites that loaded a staging script from Amazon CloudFront and handed clicks to a TDS. The TDS scripts were in place by December 2025; malware distribution through them began in January 2026. In other words, the pipes were already in place weeks before anyone turned on the malware tap. The chains were always long. Now they are selective. Long redirect chains are stale news. A USENIX Security study back from 2008 found that in half of the cases where malware was delivered through ads, the visitor passed more than six redirects before reaching the payload. What has changed is selectivity, and Coruna takes it to the extreme. A mismatched exploit crashes Safari, and a chain delivered to a researcher gets patched. If a reviewer visits once, from one profile, they see exactly the version the attacker wanted them to see. What an advertising platform sees, and when An ad platform cannot see an infected device, but it sees what endpoint tools never do, in three windows: At submission: account signals, the declared destination, domain history, and reuse of domains, scripts or hosting from blocked campaigns. At moderation: the full redirect path, scripts and hidden iframes on the landing page, and whether the page answers different visitor profiles differently. After launch: real traffic, destination changes after approval, and abuse reports. Visibility also has edges. In one ADEX case , the ad itself ended at a Google search page. The critical hop happened only after the user clicked the first result, pushing the next stage outside the ad’s direct click path. That is exactly why destination verification and journey reconstruction are not the same thing. None of this requires catching the payload red-handed. A page that loads a hidden iframe, checks the OS version and calls a version-specific script is suspicious before anyone retrieves the exploit. One operator, fifty faces Everything above about Coruna comes from GTIG’s research. What follows is ADEX’s own investigation, and it concerns the delivery method, not the exploit kit: ADEX found ad campaigns built on the same qualify-first logic, which does not mean Coruna itself was delivered through them. The ADEX team identified approximately 50 advertiser accounts linked to campaigns that used the similar delivery setup behind landing pages with nothing in common: a social offer, a finance page, changing formats and verticals. The findings were passed to the platforms using ADEX, whose teams reviewed the accounts and took action. Underneath, the chain was identical. A hidden iframe checked the OS version. An orchestrator then filtered out bots and crawlers, checked the IP, and served a script for that iOS version as an ordinary-looking .min.js file. That sequence is what linked the accounts. Nothing on the pages themselves connected them: themes, brands, verticals and formats all differed. Only the delivery behavior repeated. Creative by creative, these looked like unrelated advertisers. By delivery behavior, they looked like one operator. The cloaking setup takes weeks to build; a landing page takes a day, so operators reuse the first and refresh the second. The analysis gave ADEX metrics that now flag the pattern during moderation, before a campaign reaches traffic. A new campaign that reproduces the delivery pattern is flagged whatever its landing page looks like. What changed in 2026 ADEX’s Trust & Safety review, based on moderation data from eight ad platforms for January to September 2026, shows the same shift at scale. Indicator Earlier period Q3 2026 Cloaking, share of suspensions ~75% (full year 2025) ~45% Malicious iOS scripts, share of suspensions not a separate category before Q3 ~20% Infected domains, share of rejections ~1/3 (Q1 2026) ~1/3 Source: ADEX, State of Ad Fraud 2026: Trust & Safety Report Baseline periods differ by row, so the table shows a changing mix of reasons, not a like-for-like trend. Malicious iOS scripts became a separate category only in Q3: ~20% is their share that quarter, not measured growth. Cloaking is still the top suspension reason, but it now shares the list with device-specific scripts and messenger phishing, where persuasion moves into a chat reviewers cannot follow. AI speeds up the cheap layer: in the cases ADEX reviewed, a rejected campaign could return rebuilt within hours. The delivery infrastructure changes far more slowly, which makes it the more reliable thing to track. From “what ran” to “how the victim arrived” Endpoint detection remains necessary, but it starts at the last step of the chain and treats incidents separately, even when one delivery path sits behind several. Level What the team does Question it answers Blind spot 1. Payload-centric Endpoint alerts, hashes, IOC blocklists What ran? How the victim got there 2. Path reconstruction Rebuilds the redirect chain from DNS, proxy and browser data after an incident Where did it come from? Reactive; one chain at a time 3. Delivery-aware Clusters incidents by delivery traits; rescans from varied profiles What else uses this path? No view of traffic sources 4. Upstream-connected Shares path-level signals with ad platforms and traffic sources Who is being sent down this path now? — Moving up does not require a new product, only a few changes in practice: Record the path, not only the file. The redirect chain is often the only artifact shared by incidents that look unrelated. Treat a single clean crawl as inconclusive. Revisit suspicious paths from different device and network profiles, and follow the journey beyond the declared destination. A clean first hop may simply hand the user off to the next stage. Cluster by delivery, not content. Redirect shape, iframe behavior, script hashes and hosting survive a creative refresh; page themes do not. Keep legacy devices in view. Apple backported Coruna-relevant fixes to iOS 15.8.7 in March 2026, but unpatched devices stay exposed longest. Report the full path to the source. An ad platform can block an operator’s next fifty campaigns only if it sees what connects them. The takeaway The layer that decides which visitor is real and which is a reviewer is the same engineering whether it protects an exploit chain or a scam page. “What ran?” remains a necessary question. Teams that also ask “how did the victim arrive?” see the operator earlier and connect incidents that otherwise look unrelated. Methodology ADEX figures come from the State of Ad Fraud 2026: Trust & Safety Report, based on aggregated moderation data from ad platforms using ADEX, January to September 2026. Percentages describe the composition of rejected or suspended campaigns in that dataset, not industry-wide prevalence. Author: Farukh Rakhimov — Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding, the parent company of ADEX. Over 8 years he has built and led compliance, data protection, and information security across the group. His work spans GDPR governance, KYC and AML frameworks, financial risk assessment, and ISO 27001 certification for the group’s flagship platforms. A PhD candidate at the University of Cyprus, Farukh brings a practical, no-nonsense take on data protection — showing how businesses can turn regulatory pressure into real trust and treat compliance as a competitive edge, not a checkbox.
items.summary_html:
By Farukh Rakhimov, Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding

In March 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) disclosed Coruna, an iOS exploit kit with five exploit chains and 23 exploits covering iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1.

The most instructive part of the disclosure is what happened before the exploit got any chance to run.

Coruna was amazingly picky about visitors. A JavaScript fingerprinting module checked whether the visitor was a real device, which iPhone model it was and which iOS version it ran. Only then did the framework fire a matching exploit.

Researchers, scanners, Lockdown Mode devices and private browsing sessions were shown the door.

For a defender, the payload is where the investigation starts. For the operator, it is the end of the assembly line: by then, traffic has already been acquired, routed and qualified, mostly in plain view.

At PropellerAds, we see that upstream layer from the advertising side, including through ADEX, our traffic-quality and anti-fraud system.

A malware campaign is a delivery system

A modern malware campaign makes a lot more sense if you look at it as a delivery system. It usually has five parts:

  • Acquisition: a paid ad, a search result, a compromised site, a messenger link.
  • Routing: redirectors and traffic distribution systems (TDS) that decide where each visitor goes next.
  • Trusted infrastructure: CDNs, code repositories and file-sharing services that help malicious traffic blend into the furniture well.
  • Visitor qualification: fingerprinting that decides who gets the payload and who gets a decoy.
  • Persuasion: a fake download page, a fake virus alert, or a chat in WhatsApp or Telegram.

In June 2026, Check Point Research described fake open-source download sites that loaded a staging script from Amazon CloudFront and handed clicks to a TDS.

The TDS scripts were in place by December 2025; malware distribution through them began in January 2026. In other words, the pipes were already in place weeks before anyone turned on the malware tap.

The chains were always long. Now they are selective.

Long redirect chains are stale news. A USENIX Security study back from 2008 found that in half of the cases where malware was delivered through ads, the visitor passed more than six redirects before reaching the payload.

What has changed is selectivity, and Coruna takes it to the extreme. A mismatched exploit crashes Safari, and a chain delivered to a researcher gets patched. If a reviewer visits once, from one profile, they see exactly the version the attacker wanted them to see. 

What an advertising platform sees, and when

An ad platform cannot see an infected device, but it sees what endpoint tools never do, in three windows:

  • At submission: account signals, the declared destination, domain history, and reuse of domains, scripts or hosting from blocked campaigns.
  • At moderation: the full redirect path, scripts and hidden iframes on the landing page, and whether the page answers different visitor profiles differently.
  • After launch: real traffic, destination changes after approval, and abuse reports.

Visibility also has edges. In one ADEX case, the ad itself ended at a Google search page. The critical hop happened only after the user clicked the first result, pushing the next stage outside the ad’s direct click path.

That is exactly why destination verification and journey reconstruction are not the same thing. 

None of this requires catching the payload red-handed. A page that loads a hidden iframe, checks the OS version and calls a version-specific script is suspicious before anyone retrieves the exploit.

One operator, fifty faces

Everything above about Coruna comes from GTIG’s research. What follows is ADEX’s own investigation, and it concerns the delivery method, not the exploit kit: ADEX found ad campaigns built on the same qualify-first logic, which does not mean Coruna itself was delivered through them.

The ADEX team identified approximately 50 advertiser accounts linked to campaigns that used the similar delivery setup behind landing pages with nothing in common: a social offer, a finance page, changing formats and verticals.

The findings were passed to the platforms using ADEX, whose teams reviewed the accounts and took action.

Underneath, the chain was identical. A hidden iframe checked the OS version. An orchestrator then filtered out bots and crawlers, checked the IP, and served a script for that iOS version as an ordinary-looking .min.js file.

That sequence is what linked the accounts. Nothing on the pages themselves connected them: themes, brands, verticals and formats all differed. Only the delivery behavior repeated.

Creative by creative, these looked like unrelated advertisers. By delivery behavior, they looked like one operator.

The cloaking setup takes weeks to build; a landing page takes a day, so operators reuse the first and refresh the second.

The analysis gave ADEX metrics that now flag the pattern during moderation, before a campaign reaches traffic. A new campaign that reproduces the delivery pattern is flagged whatever its landing page looks like.

What changed in 2026

ADEX’s Trust & Safety review, based on moderation data from eight ad platforms for January to September 2026, shows the same shift at scale.

IndicatorEarlier periodQ3 2026Cloaking, share of suspensions~75% (full year 2025)~45%Malicious iOS scripts, share of suspensionsnot a separate category before Q3~20%Infected domains, share of rejections~1/3 (Q1 2026)~1/3

Source: ADEX, State of Ad Fraud 2026: Trust & Safety Report

Baseline periods differ by row, so the table shows a changing mix of reasons, not a like-for-like trend. Malicious iOS scripts became a separate category only in Q3: ~20% is their share that quarter, not measured growth.

Cloaking is still the top suspension reason, but it now shares the list with device-specific scripts and messenger phishing, where persuasion moves into a chat reviewers cannot follow.

AI speeds up the cheap layer: in the cases ADEX reviewed, a rejected campaign could return rebuilt within hours. The delivery infrastructure changes far more slowly, which makes it the more reliable thing to track.

From “what ran” to “how the victim arrived”

Endpoint detection remains necessary, but it starts at the last step of the chain and treats incidents separately, even when one delivery path sits behind several.

LevelWhat the team doesQuestion it answersBlind spot1. Payload-centricEndpoint alerts, hashes, IOC blocklistsWhat ran?How the victim got there2. Path reconstructionRebuilds the redirect chain from DNS, proxy and browser data after an incidentWhere did it come from?Reactive; one chain at a time3. Delivery-awareClusters incidents by delivery traits; rescans from varied profilesWhat else uses this path?No view of traffic sources4. Upstream-connectedShares path-level signals with ad platforms and traffic sourcesWho is being sent down this path now?—

Moving up does not require a new product, only a few changes in practice:

  • Record the path, not only the file. The redirect chain is often the only artifact shared by incidents that look unrelated.
  • Treat a single clean crawl as inconclusive. Revisit suspicious paths from different device and network profiles, and follow the journey beyond the declared destination. A clean first hop may simply hand the user off to the next stage. 
  • Cluster by delivery, not content. Redirect shape, iframe behavior, script hashes and hosting survive a creative refresh; page themes do not.
  • Keep legacy devices in view. Apple backported Coruna-relevant fixes to iOS 15.8.7 in March 2026, but unpatched devices stay exposed longest. 
  • Report the full path to the source. An ad platform can block an operator’s next fifty campaigns only if it sees what connects them.
The takeaway

The layer that decides which visitor is real and which is a reviewer is the same engineering whether it protects an exploit chain or a scam page. “What ran?” remains a necessary question.

Teams that also ask “how did the victim arrive?” see the operator earlier and connect incidents that otherwise look unrelated.

Methodology

ADEX figures come from the State of Ad Fraud 2026: Trust & Safety Report, based on aggregated moderation data from ad platforms using ADEX, January to September 2026.

Percentages describe the composition of rejected or suspended campaigns in that dataset, not industry-wide prevalence.

Author:

Farukh Rakhimov — Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding, the parent company of ADEX. Over 8 years he has built and led compliance, data protection, and information security across the group. His work spans GDPR governance, KYC and AML frameworks, financial risk assessment, and ISO 27001 certification for the group’s flagship platforms. A PhD candidate at the University of Cyprus, Farukh brings a practical, no-nonsense take on data protection — showing how businesses can turn regulatory pressure into real trust and treat compliance as a competitive edge, not a checkbox.

items.title: OWASP Finds ChatGPT Helped Low-Skilled User Take Over Admin Account in Hacking Test
items.summary: OWASP found that ChatGPT helped an operator with no offensive security knowledge take over an administrator account during a controlled hacking test . The operator largely copied commands, returned results to the chatbot, and followed its guidance to change a password and log in. The finding shows how AI can lower the skill needed for some attacks without removing the need for human input. The LLM Exploit Generation Phase 2 report , published by the OWASP GenAI Security Project, compared human-guided chat sessions with autonomous agents against live Hack The Box targets. These were authorized training environments, not breached businesses. Researchers tracked success, human effort, costs, safety controls, and failures. The main test involved Silentium, a machine with a hidden staging website running a vulnerable version of Flowise . Using a testing guide generated by ChatGPT, the operator followed instructions with the common security tools nmap and curl. ChatGPT directed information gathering and uncovered the staging site, which the operator would not have known to investigate. It then identified a login flow that revealed valid usernames and guided the operator through changing an administrator account’s password. The operator confirmed the takeover by signing in with the new credentials. OWASP Finds ChatGPT-Assisted Admin Takeover The result was not entirely skill-free. The test persona allowed general computer literacy, command-line use, and intermediate prompting ability. The operator also had to recognize refusals and reframe requests as authorized testing. Installing the Kali environment was outside the test’s scope. Researchers also observed a response disappearing behind an error before a repeated request succeeded. They could not confirm the cause or reproduce the event, so it does not establish a general weakness in OpenAI’s safeguards. The autonomous track tested nine configurations using CAI, HexStrike, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and hosted or local models. Stronger multi-agent setups discovered staging sites, identified vulnerable software, and researched exploit paths with little guidance after setup. However, no autonomous run completed the final Silentium takeover step. Provider safety controls stopped the hosted systems that reached that stage, leaving humans to finish. Other runs stalled in repeated scans, password-cracking loops, hostname errors, or tool failures. This distinction adds context to broader reporting on hackers using autonomous AI agents . In OWASP’s tests, the software around the model often mattered more than model choice, and building that software required expertise. Costs also extended beyond API bills. Productive hosted runs cost tens of dollars, but setup, troubleshooting, and supervision remained important. A local Qwen Coder run avoided API charges yet needed repeated human corrections and ended with a tool integration error. OWASP identified repeated, similar scans and requests against one target as a possible detection signal. Human-guided activity could be quieter, although the study did not directly measure stealth or detection rates. For teams deploying agents, OWASP recommends enforcing approval before high-impact actions rather than relying only on model safeguards. Related coverage of hijacked AI pentesting agents highlights why those controls matter. The report also warns against treating benchmark scores as proof of real-world hacking ability. Its small sample supports a narrower conclusion: AI speeds up parts of an attack, but reliable execution still depends on people. Give your SOC the alert context to stop incidents quickly. OWASP found that ChatGPT helped an operator with no offensive security knowledge take over an administrator account during a controlled hacking test.

The operator largely copied commands, returned results to the chatbot, and followed its guidance to change a password and log in. The finding shows how AI can lower the skill needed for some attacks without removing the need for human input.

The LLM Exploit Generation Phase 2 report, published by the OWASP GenAI Security Project, compared human-guided chat sessions with autonomous agents against live Hack The Box targets.

These were authorized training environments, not breached businesses. Researchers tracked success, human effort, costs, safety controls, and failures.

The main test involved Silentium, a machine with a hidden staging website running a vulnerable version of Flowise. Using a testing guide generated by ChatGPT, the operator followed instructions with the common security tools nmap and curl.

ChatGPT directed information gathering and uncovered the staging site, which the operator would not have known to investigate. It then identified a login flow that revealed valid usernames and guided the operator through changing an administrator account’s password. The operator confirmed the takeover by signing in with the new credentials.

OWASP Finds ChatGPT-Assisted Admin Takeover

The result was not entirely skill-free. The test persona allowed general computer literacy, command-line use, and intermediate prompting ability. The operator also had to recognize refusals and reframe requests as authorized testing. Installing the Kali environment was outside the test’s scope.

Researchers also observed a response disappearing behind an error before a repeated request succeeded. They could not confirm the cause or reproduce the event, so it does not establish a general weakness in OpenAI’s safeguards.

The autonomous track tested nine configurations using CAI, HexStrike, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and hosted or local models. Stronger multi-agent setups discovered staging sites, identified vulnerable software, and researched exploit paths with little guidance after setup.

However, no autonomous run completed the final Silentium takeover step. Provider safety controls stopped the hosted systems that reached that stage, leaving humans to finish. Other runs stalled in repeated scans, password-cracking loops, hostname errors, or tool failures.

This distinction adds context to broader reporting on hackers using autonomous AI agents. In OWASP’s tests, the software around the model often mattered more than model choice, and building that software required expertise.

Costs also extended beyond API bills. Productive hosted runs cost tens of dollars, but setup, troubleshooting, and supervision remained important. A local Qwen Coder run avoided API charges yet needed repeated human corrections and ended with a tool integration error.

OWASP identified repeated, similar scans and requests against one target as a possible detection signal. Human-guided activity could be quieter, although the study did not directly measure stealth or detection rates.

For teams deploying agents, OWASP recommends enforcing approval before high-impact actions rather than relying only on model safeguards. Related coverage of hijacked AI pentesting agents highlights why those controls matter.

The report also warns against treating benchmark scores as proof of real-world hacking ability. Its small sample supports a narrower conclusion: AI speeds up parts of an attack, but reliable execution still depends on people.
