items.summary: by Chad Gish Key takeaways OSINT, or open-source intelligence, is information gathered from publicly available sources such as social media, websites, forums, and public records. Public information and physical device forensics are strongest when used together. OSINT can identify suspects, accounts, and locations early, and device evidence can then validate, expand, or challenge those findings. Investigators can often access OSINT before any other digital evidence, since it doesn’t depend on locating and lawfully acquiring a device or waiting on a provider. No single source of digital evidence tells the whole story. OSINT is one of six pillars alongside physical devices, cloud data, video, cell site information, and vehicle infotainment data, and the value comes from the connections between them. Open-source intelligence, or OSINT, and physical device forensics work best when investigators use them together. Open-source intelligence can help identify suspects, accounts, aliases, locations, and relationships early in an investigation, while physical device evidence can help validate, expand, or challenge what was first found through publicly available information. Over the years, I’ve come to think about digital evidence in terms of what I call the six pillars of digital forensics : Physical devices Video Cloud data OSINT Cell site information and call detail records (CDR) Vehicle infotainment data Each pillar can provide valuable information on its own, but in my experience, the real power comes from understanding how those pillars work together. One source of digital evidence can create the lead that points investigators to another, and information from one pillar can help corroborate what was found in another. In this article, I want to focus on two of those pillars, OSINT and physical devices, and how they can work together to help investigators develop leads, establish timelines, identify suspects, and build a stronger evidentiary picture. Why physical devices aren’t always the first evidence available When investigators think about digital evidence, physical devices are often one of the first things that come to mind. A suspect’s cellphone, computer, tablet, or other device can contain an incredible amount of information about that person’s activities, communications, relationships, movements, and interests. But there’s often a gap between knowing that evidence may exist and actually being able to examine it. A device has to be located and lawfully acquired. A search warrant may need to be obtained. The device has to be preserved, extracted, and processed before an examiner can begin analyzing the information it contains. Cloud data can present similar challenges when investigators need legal process and have to wait for a provider to respond. That is where OSINT can become particularly valuable. What is OSINT in a digital forensics investigation? Open-source intelligence (OSINT) is information collected from publicly available sources and analyzed to develop investigative intelligence. It can include publicly accessible social media accounts and posts, websites, photographs, videos, online forums, public records, usernames, geospatial data, aliases, and many other sources of information available on the internet. Social media is often the richest of these sources, and the subset of OSINT focused on it is called social media intelligence, or SOCMINT . The important distinction is that OSINT is based on information that is publicly available. It does not mean hacking into an account, bypassing security, or obtaining information that requires unauthorized access. For investigators, one of the greatest advantages of OSINT is that it can sometimes be available before other forms of digital evidence can be obtained. That can be especially important early in a criminal investigation, when investigators may know that a person is involved but may not know the person’s real name, address, phone number, social media accounts, or even where that person lives. This is common in cases involving individuals who intentionally avoid using their real identifying information. In those situations, investigators have to look at the information they do have and ask a simple question: What can I do with it? Sometimes the answer is a nickname. How OSINT can turn a nickname into an investigative lead I experienced this firsthand during a homicide investigation where one of the only active investigative leads was a very unique nickname associated with the suspect. That may not sound like much. In a traditional investigation, a nickname can seem almost useless without a last name, address, date of birth, or other identifying information. But in this case, the nickname was unusual enough that it became the starting point for an OSINT investigation. Using that nickname, I searched publicly available social media platforms. The nickname led to an account, the account led to a person, and that person turned out to be the suspect investigators were looking for. That discovery was important, but identifying the suspect was only the beginning. The real value came from continuing to follow the information and looking at the digital trail surrounding that individual. Public information helped establish additional identifiers, including an address and other details that could be used to begin piecing together the suspect’s whereabouts before and after the homicide. Individually, some of the information may not have seemed particularly significant. Taken together, however, it began to establish a timeline and provided information that was relevant to the homicide investigation. That is one of the things I find most valuable about OSINT. The value is not always in finding one piece of information that solves the case. More often, it comes from finding multiple pieces of information and understanding how they relate to one another. A nickname can lead to a social media account. A social media account can lead to an identity. An identity can lead to an address. An address can lead investigators to a physical device. Information from that device can then be compared with what was first discovered through OSINT. That is where the pillars begin to connect. How OSINT fits inside the digital evidence workflow One thing I appreciate about today’s digital forensic environment is that OSINT does not have to exist as a completely separate investigative process. Public-facing information found online can become part of the broader digital evidence workflow. Magnet Axiom’s cloud capabilities allow investigators to acquire and analyze publicly available information from supported social media platforms and incorporate that information into an Axiom case. Depending on the platform and current capabilities, this can include public-facing information from services such as Facebook, Instagram, and X. For example, an investigator may start with a username or nickname. That information may lead to a public social media account, which can provide more context about the person, their relationships, activities, locations, or online presence. That public information can then be acquired through the appropriate Axiom cloud workflow and examined alongside other evidence in the same case environment. This is the role Magnet Axiom plays. OSINT may help investigators find the thread, but Axiom helps them follow that thread across devices, accounts, artifacts, conversations, locations, and timelines. Instead of looking at public-facing information in one place and physical device evidence in another, investigators can bring those sources together, compare them, and begin building a more complete evidentiary picture. OSINT does not replace physical device forensics It’s important to make one thing clear: OSINT is not a replacement for physical device forensics, cloud data, cell site information, video, or the other pillars of digital evidence. It’s another source of evidence and investigative intelligence. One of the biggest mistakes investigators can make is looking at these sources independently. Digital evidence rarely exists in a vacuum. A cellphone may contain information that points back to social media. A social media account may help identify a cellphone or other device. Video, cell site information, cloud data, and vehicle infotainment data may each provide another layer of context. The individual pillars become much more valuable when investigators look for the connections between them. That is particularly true with OSINT and physical devices. From OSINT to physical device evidence and back again Once investigators have identified a suspect through OSINT, the investigation can change significantly. Instead of searching for an unknown person, investigators may now have a name, address, associated accounts, telephone number, vehicle information, or other identifiers. Those details can be used to develop additional investigative leads and, when appropriate, support the legal process necessary to obtain physical devices and other non-public digital evidence. This is where the transition from OSINT to physical device evidence becomes important. A smartphone can contain communications, photographs, browser history, application data, location-related artifacts, social media information, contacts, documents, and countless other pieces of information. A computer can provide an entirely different view of a person’s digital activity. Using Magnet Graykey for mobile device extractions and Magnet Axiom for processing and analysis, investigators and forensic examiners can examine the data recovered from physical devices and place that information into the broader context of the investigation. The question is no longer simply, “What’s on this phone?” The better question is, “How does what’s on this phone relate to everything else we already know?” Suppose OSINT establishes that a particular social media account belongs to a suspect. When a physical device is later examined, investigators may find that same account, username, email address, communications, photographs, or other artifacts on the device. What began as publicly available information can now be examined alongside forensic evidence recovered from the device. The reverse can also happen when a device examination reveals a username, email address, phone number, photograph, website, or other identifier that sends investigators back into additional OSINT research. Connecting OSINT, mobile device forensics, and other digital evidence This is also where forensic platforms become increasingly important. Modern investigations can involve enormous amounts of data from multiple sources, and acquiring the data is only the first step. Investigators have to process it, search it, understand it, and determine how individual artifacts relate to one another. For example, imagine an investigator develops a suspect’s identity through OSINT. That information leads to a physical address and eventually to the seizure of a cellphone. The device is extracted with Graykey and processed in Axiom. The examiner may find communications that establish relationships with other individuals, photographs that provide additional context, application artifacts that establish activity, and other information that helps build a timeline. That information can then be compared with the OSINT that initially identified the suspect. If the investigation also involves video, cell site information, vehicle infotainment data, or cloud records, those sources can be evaluated against the same timeline. Suddenly, investigators are no longer looking at isolated pieces of digital evidence. They are looking at corroborating evidence from multiple pillars. Explaining OSINT and device evidence in the courtroom Finding information is only part of the investigation. Investigators also need to explain where the information came from, how it was obtained and preserved, and why it should be considered reliable. That applies to OSINT just as much as physical device evidence. With OSINT, investigators should be prepared to explain the source of the information, how it was attributed to a person or account, when it was collected, and how it was preserved. Publicly available information can still be inaccurate, misleading, impersonated, or difficult to attribute, so those issues need to be considered early. Physical device evidence carries its own requirements. Investigators and examiners must be able to explain the legal authority, extraction process, tools used, artifacts recovered, and how those artifacts were interpreted. The strongest digital evidence is often the evidence that can be corroborated by another source. A social media post, cellphone artifact, video clip, cloud record, cell site record, or vehicle infotainment artifact may each tell part of the story. When those sources independently support the same conclusion, the evidentiary picture becomes stronger and easier to explain. The six pillars are stronger together Technology continues to change the way people communicate, travel, work, and interact with the world around them. As a result, investigators have more potential sources of digital evidence than ever before. The challenge is recognizing where that evidence exists and understanding how the different sources can work together. That is why I continue to look at digital evidence through the lens of the six pillars. OSINT may be the first pillar an investigator can access. A physical device may provide the most detailed view of an individual’s digital activity. Cloud data may fill in information that is missing from the device. Video may corroborate a location or activity. Cell site information may help establish where a device was during a particular period. Vehicle infotainment data may provide another independent source of location and activity information. No single pillar necessarily tells the entire story. When investigators learn to move between the pillars, the individual pieces of information begin to make more sense. That homicide investigation started with something that, on its face, did not appear to be much: a nickname. That nickname led to OSINT. OSINT led to an identity. The identity led to an address and additional information about the suspect. From there, the investigation could continue into the other pillars of digital evidence. That is the lesson I continue to take from these investigations: don’t underestimate the value of the first piece of information you have, no matter how insignificant it may seem. In today’s digital environment, a nickname, username, photograph, or public social media post may be the first piece of information that moves an investigation forward. The real value comes from what investigators do next: validating that lead, connecting it to other sources of evidence, and building a timeline that can be clearly explained. Magnet Axiom helps investigators bring OSINT, physical device evidence, cloud data, communications, media, and timelines together so they can move from a single lead to a stronger, more complete case. Frequently asked questions What is OSINT in digital forensics? OSINT, or open-source intelligence, is publicly available information investigators use to develop leads, identify people or accounts, and add context to a digital investigation. How does OSINT support physical device forensics? OSINT can identify a suspect, username, phone number, address, or account that helps investigators pursue and examine a physical device. Device artifacts can then be compared with the original OSINT findings. How does Magnet Axiom help connect OSINT and device evidence? Magnet Axiom helps investigators process, search, analyze, and connect OSINT, mobile device data, computer artifacts, cloud evidence, communications, media, and timelines in one case. Why is it important to combine multiple digital evidence sources? Corroborating OSINT, physical devices, cloud data, video, cell site information, and vehicle infotainment data helps investigators build a clearer, stronger, and more defensible timeline. About the author Chad Gish, Senior Principal Forensic Specialist at Magnet Forensics, is a retired police detective with more than 25 years of experience investigating homicides, mass casualty events, and crimes against children. He is a recognized expert in digital forensics, playing a key role in high-profile cases and the development of forensic labs and crime centers.

The device has to be preserved, extracted, and processed before an examiner can begin analyzing the information it contains. That is where OSINT can become particularly valuable.

Open-source intelligence (OSINT) is information collected from publicly available sources and analyzed to develop investigative intelligence. It can include publicly accessible social media accounts and posts, websites, photographs, videos, online forums, public records, usernames, geospatial data, aliases, and many other sources of information available on the internet. items.title: CVE-2026-115881: Critical GoAhead TLS Flaw Allows Revoked Client Certificates
items.summary: A critical vulnerability in the GoAhead embedded web server can allow revoked client certificates to remain valid during mutual TLS authentication, potentially giving previously trusted identities continued access to protected devices and services. Tracked as CVE-2026-115881, the flaw carries a vendor-assigned CVSS score of 9.1 and affects GoAhead versions 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 when the software uses its OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend with certificate revocation lists configured. The issue was fixed in GoAhead 6.1.1. GoAhead is an embedded web server commonly integrated into routers, printers, gateways, industrial systems, and other network-connected products. However, the vulnerability does not affect every GoAhead installation. Exploitation requires a specific mutual TLS configuration, and the affected population of commercial devices has not been established. The vulnerability stems from improper certificate revocation validation. GoAhead successfully loads a configured Certificate Revocation List (CRL) into OpenSSL’s certificate store, but fails to activate the OpenSSL flag required to enforce CRL checking. Consequently, a certificate explicitly marked as revoked can still complete authentication. For CVE-2026-115881 detection, security teams should combine software inventory, TLS backend identification, certificate telemetry, and monitoring of mutual TLS authentication. Because an affected server treats the revoked certificate as valid, exploitation may not generate an obvious authentication failure or traditional exploit signature. SOC Prime users can strengthen coverage for exploitation attempts and suspicious post-authentication behavior by correlating identity, network, application, and endpoint telemetry across their security stack. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-115881, defenders should first identify vulnerable GoAhead deployments and then monitor for authentication performed with certificates that should already have been revoked. Contact Sales CVE-2026-115881 analysis The vulnerability exists in the way GoAhead integrates Certificate Revocation List validation with its OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend. In mutual TLS, both sides authenticate using digital certificates. Organizations can revoke a client certificate when a device is retired, an employee loses access, a private key is compromised, or the associated identity should otherwise no longer be trusted. A CRL provides the server with a list of certificates that must be rejected. Researchers at FoxIO found that GoAhead correctly loads the configured CRL using OpenSSL, but fails to enable the X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK verification flag. Loading a CRL into the certificate store alone does not cause OpenSSL to check certificate revocation status. items.summary_html:
A critical vulnerability in the GoAhead embedded web server can allow revoked client certificates to remain valid during mutual TLS authentication, potentially giving previously trusted identities continued access to protected devices and services.

Tracked as CVE-2026-115881, the flaw carries a vendor-assigned CVSS score of 9.1 and affects GoAhead versions 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 when the software uses its OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend with certificate revocation lists configured. The issue was fixed in GoAhead 6.1.1.

GoAhead is an embedded web server commonly integrated into routers, printers, gateways, industrial systems, and other network-connected products. However, the vulnerability does not affect every GoAhead installation. Exploitation requires a specific mutual TLS configuration, and the affected population of commercial devices has not been established.

The vulnerability stems from improper certificate revocation validation. GoAhead successfully loads a configured Certificate Revocation List (CRL) into OpenSSL’s certificate store, but fails to activate the OpenSSL flag required to enforce CRL checking. Consequently, a certificate explicitly marked as revoked can still complete authentication.

For CVE-2026-115881 detection, security teams should combine software inventory, TLS backend identification, certificate telemetry, and monitoring of mutual TLS authentication. Because an affected server treats the revoked certificate as valid, exploitation may not generate an obvious authentication failure or traditional exploit signature.

SOC Prime users can strengthen coverage for exploitation attempts and suspicious post-authentication behavior by correlating identity, network, application, and endpoint telemetry across their security stack.

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-115881, defenders should first identify vulnerable GoAhead deployments and then monitor for authentication performed with certificates that should already have been revoked.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-115881 analysis

The vulnerability exists in the way GoAhead integrates Certificate Revocation List validation with its OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend.

In mutual TLS, both sides authenticate using digital certificates. Organizations can revoke a client certificate when a device is retired, an employee loses access, a private key is compromised, or the associated identity should otherwise no longer be trusted.

A CRL provides the server with a list of certificates that must be rejected.

Researchers at FoxIO found that GoAhead correctly loads the configured CRL using OpenSSL, but fails to enable the X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK verification flag. Loading a CRL into the certificate store alone does not cause OpenSSL to check certificate revocation status.

As a result, certificate verification can complete successfully even when the client certificate appears on the configured revocation list.

FoxIO reproduced the issue using GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2. During testing, a revoked client certificate signed by a trusted CA successfully completed an mTLS handshake even when issuer verification was enabled. The server generated no startup warning indicating that revocation checking was ineffective.

This silent failure is particularly significant because administrators may reasonably assume that configuring a CRL means revoked certificates will be rejected.

The details for CVE-2026-115881 show that exploitation requires several conditions to be present:

  • GoAhead must use the OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend.
  • The deployment must require client certificates.
  • A trusted CA bundle must be configured.
  • Certificate issuer verification must be enabled for the clearest security impact.
  • A CRL must be configured.
  • The attacker must possess a certificate issued by the trusted authority that has subsequently been revoked.

The flaw therefore does not represent a generic authentication bypass against default GoAhead installations.

CVE-2026-115881 affects GoAhead versions 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 using the vulnerable OpenSSL-compatible code path with a CRL configured. GoAhead 6.1.1 corrects the issue by enabling CRL checking after the revocation list is loaded.

The attack scenario is most relevant when an adversary already possesses a formerly valid certificate. For example, a stolen device certificate could remain usable even after administrators revoke it. The attacker could then authenticate to whatever management interface, API, or protected resource that certificate identity is authorized to access.

Because the certificate is cryptographically valid and signed by the expected CA, ordinary certificate-chain validation does not necessarily expose the attack. The missing control is specifically revocation enforcement.

FoxIO has published a CVE-2026-115881 PoC as part of its technical research, demonstrating the vulnerable certificate-validation behavior. The researchers also published JA4Scan fingerprints that can help organizations identify GoAhead installations and distinguish TLS backends.

Those fingerprints are useful for exposure discovery, but they should not be treated as proof that a device is vulnerable. TLS fingerprinting can indicate that a server resembles a particular GoAhead/backend combination, while actual exposure still depends on version and compile-time configuration.

The critical OpenSSL issue was disclosed alongside two additional GoAhead TLS weaknesses.

A separate issue tracked as CVE-2026-115884 affects older LibreSSL verifier behavior and can allow an over-depth certificate chain to bypass GoAhead’s chain-depth restriction under a specific configuration where client certificates are required but issuer verification is disabled.

Another flaw affects GoAhead builds using Mbed TLS. A buffer-length mistake can reduce a configured 2048-bit Diffie-Hellman modulus to a single byte during certain TLS 1.2 DHE_RSA handshakes, potentially allowing a passive observer to recover session keys when a client accepts the malformed parameters.

These are separate vulnerabilities with different prerequisites. They should not be conflated with CVE-2026-115881 when assessing exposure.

FoxIO’s disclosure timeline states that the OpenSSL CRL issue was reported on April 30, 2026. GoAhead 6.1.1 containing the fix was released to device builders on August 2, while the security advisories became public on October 12. FoxIO published its detailed technical research on October 26.

As of October 28, 2026, there are no reports in the supplied sources of CVE-2026-115881 being exploited in real-world attacks.

Consequently, there are no campaign-specific CVE-2026-115881 IOCs such as confirmed malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or exploit infrastructure associated with in-the-wild exploitation.

Defenders should instead focus on exposure and behavioral indicators:

  • GoAhead versions between 3.4.5 and 6.1.0
  • OpenSSL-compatible TLS backend
  • Mutual TLS enabled
  • A configured Certificate Revocation List
  • Authentication using certificates whose serial numbers appear on the organization’s CRL
  • Unexpected access from retired or compromised device identities
  • Sensitive administrative activity following certificate-based authentication
  • New configuration changes or credential creation originating from embedded management interfaces
  • Network access to management services from unexpected locations

Organizations using centralized PKI should also correlate TLS authentication with certificate lifecycle information. A successful authentication event involving a certificate already marked as revoked is a high-value signal regardless of whether the underlying service is GoAhead.

CVE-2026-115881 Mitigation

The primary remediation is upgrading GoAhead to version 6.1.1 or later.

The patched release enables OpenSSL CRL enforcement after loading the configured revocation list, causing certificates listed as revoked to be rejected during validation.

For organizations developing products directly with GoAhead, updating the embedded server component should be prioritized before new firmware or software builds are distributed.

The situation is more complicated for end users operating commercial routers, gateways, printers, industrial equipment, or other appliances containing GoAhead.

GoAhead is generally embedded inside vendor firmware. Updating the upstream GoAhead project does not automatically update installed devices. Equipment owners therefore need to obtain a firmware release from the manufacturer that incorporates GoAhead 6.1.1 or a vendor-provided equivalent fix.

The recommended CVE-2026-115881 mitigation process should include:

  • Inventory devices and applications that may embed GoAhead.
  • Determine the installed GoAhead version where possible.
  • Identify whether the product uses OpenSSL, Mbed TLS, LibreSSL, or another supported backend.
  • Determine whether mutual TLS authentication is enabled.
  • Check whether a CRL is configured.
  • Contact device manufacturers to confirm whether their products include the vulnerable implementation.
  • Apply firmware containing GoAhead 6.1.1 or a vendor-specific fix as soon as it becomes available.
  • Restrict access to administrative and management interfaces.
  • Limit management services to trusted networks, VPNs, or dedicated administrative segments.
  • Review the status of all client certificates authorized to authenticate to affected devices.

Organizations should not assume that the presence of a CRL proves revocation is functioning correctly.

Where operationally practical, administrators can test their own infrastructure by revoking a dedicated test certificate and verifying that the device refuses the subsequent mTLS connection. Production certificates should not be used for this validation.

If immediate patching is impossible, network isolation becomes particularly important. Management interfaces exposed to untrusted networks should be restricted using firewall rules, segmentation, access control lists, or dedicated management networks.

Organizations should also review their PKI environment for certificates revoked because of suspected private-key compromise. Those credentials represent the highest-priority risk because an attacker possessing the corresponding private key may still be able to authenticate to vulnerable services.

If compromise is suspected, revoke or replace affected credentials, rotate related secrets, inspect administrative changes, and investigate activity performed under the certificate identity.

Security teams should additionally review device configuration changes, account creation, firmware modifications, authentication records, and outbound connections that occurred after suspicious certificate-based access.

The other GoAhead TLS vulnerabilities disclosed alongside CVE-2026-115881 require separate remediation considerations.

Mbed TLS deployments affected by the Diffie-Hellman issue can upgrade to 6.1.1, disable finite-field DHE cipher suites, or migrate to the OpenSSL backend. LibreSSL deployments affected by CVE-2026-115884 can upgrade GoAhead, enable issuer checking with a trusted CA bundle, or migrate to a newer LibreSSL or OpenSSL implementation.

Ultimately, device manufacturers need to rebuild affected firmware with the corrected GoAhead version before many end users can apply the fix. Organizations operating IoT, OT, network infrastructure, or embedded devices should therefore track vendor advisories rather than relying solely on the upstream GoAhead release.

items.summary: Politicians in Europe and the U.S. are speaking out against the use of advertising technology to infect targets with zero-click spyware. Following recent findings from the Citizen Lab, members of the European Parliament signed a letter urging the E.U. to investigate the potential exposure of its institutions to zero-click spyware through online targeted advertising. items.title: Google Fixes 52 Chrome Security Flaws, Including Four Critical Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Google released a Chrome security update that fixes 52 vulnerabilities, including four critical flaws affecting FileSystem, FileAPI, Skia, and Layout. According to the release notice, the Stable channel is moving to version 156.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac. At the same time, Linux users will receive version 156.0.8078.73. The update will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The supplied security list includes four critical vulnerabilities, 46 high-severity issues , and two medium-severity bugs. The fixes cover browser functions ranging from file handling and page rendering to JavaScript, graphics, video, and audio processing. CVE-2026-118306 is a memory corruption flaw in FileSystem, reported on October 7 by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic with assistance from Claude. The second critical issue, CVE-2026-118331, involves improper input validation in FileAPI. Ge reported that vulnerability on October 11, also with Claude’s assistance. The remaining critical bugs are CVE-2026-118348, an improper input validation issue in Skia, and CVE-2026-118344, a use-after-free flaw in Layout. Ge reported both on October 17. These findings highlight file operations and page display features as key areas this release addresses. A use-after-free bug occurs when software accesses memory after it has been released. Input validation flaws involve inadequate checks on incoming data. However, the supplied notice does not describe specific attack methods, confirm remote code execution, or state that attackers have exploited these vulnerabilities. Google Fixes 52 Chrome Security Flaws Google’s high-severity fixes address memory corruption, use-after-free, input validation, access control, and authorization flaws across V8, Turbolev, ANGLE, WebRTC, PDFium, WebAudio, Payments, and graphics and media components. Notable entries include CVE-2026-118318, an improper access control flaw in V8, and CVE-2026-118333, a missing authorization issue in Video. Google also fixed CVE-2026-118342, an out-of-bounds write in Editing. The notice provides no detailed exploit conditions for these issues. This release follows the earlier Chrome 156 update fixing 353 security flaws and a separate Chrome update addressing 32 vulnerabilities . These releases highlight the importance of checking the installed Chrome build rather than relying solely on the browser’s major version number. The notice credits Google researchers, independent contributors, Mozilla, Anthropic, Ada Logics, and OpenAI Codex Security. Several reports explicitly name AI assistance, although the credits do not establish that those tools independently discovered or verified every issue. items.title: FBI Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting Domain Linked to Ransomware and Cybercrime
items.summary: The FBI seized virtualine.net, the main website of a bulletproof hosting provider linked to ransomware operators, stolen-data markets, and other cybercrime services. Announced on October 27, 2026, the court-authorized action targeted a business accused of helping criminals keep their websites online, ignore abuse complaints, and hide payments. The U.S. Justice Department said Virtualine also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech. It sold hosting, servers, and domain registration services while openly seeking customers on cybercrime forums. Investigators linked its services to child sexual abuse material, the sharing of intimate images without consent, and international money laundering.s Virtualine marketed its willingness to support illegal activity as a selling point. In September 2024, it told an Exploit. user that customers could use its services for phishing, payment card fraud , spam, port scanning, and other illegal activities. Its stated exceptions were child abuse content and terrorism. By March 2026, the provider was advertising an “additional protection plan” for customers facing law enforcement requests. Under that plan, Virtualine would move a customer’s criminal infrastructure to an unrelated shell company and reactivate the server, according to court records cited by prosecutors. FBI Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting That offer shows how bulletproof hosting can help criminal operations recover from pressure rather than provide server space. Similar concerns appeared in earlier coverage of U.S. sanctions against bulletproof hosting provider Aeza , whose infrastructure supported ransomware and information-stealing malware. Chainalysis reported that Virtualine’s payment addresses were directly linked to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses. These findings provide context for the hosting provider’s role in several types of online crime. The Justice Department said Virtualine accepted payments through an option labeled “BTC [NO-AML],” using unhosted Bitcoin addresses. Prosecutors allege that Virtualine then laundered payments from criminal customers to hide their source. The announcement did not identify individual ransomware groups or disclose the total value of those transactions. A central part of the investigation involved a criminal forum identified as Vendor 1. Prosecutors say it sold access to explicit images of minors and adults and promoted hackers who could break into victims’ accounts to steal private material. Virtualine began receiving warnings about child sexual abuse material in January 2026. Notices came from police in Germany, Canada, and Australia, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, and a victim’s attorney. Despite those reports, Virtualine allegedly kept the forum online and helped build another site to upload and sell content. The FBI Washington Field Office led the investigation with German, Dutch, and British authorities, alongside OverRIPE and Lumen. The case follows wider action against criminal hosting, including U.S. charges against two bulletproof hosting companies . However, taking control of Virtualine’s domain does not establish that every related server stopped operating. Silent Push reported that Omegatech was not fully offline after the seizure. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Banks are blocking AI agents from customer accounts
items.summary: This week, Axios reported that major US banks were detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. In many cases, customers have given the agents their usernames and passwords so they could act on their behalf. This kind of access can violate a bank’s rules. Bianco Research president Jim Bianco raised the question during Unchained’s Bits + Bips livestream on October 26: “Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?” Bianco described traditional finance’s business model as “based on laziness.” Customers may leave idle cash in low- or no-interest bank accounts rather than move it into a money market fund. An AI agent could make that move for them. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said. The banks offer a different explanation. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow just any outside agent into its systems because doing so was “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.” Both explanations can be true: banks can want to retain deposits while also facing real security problems when software acts through customers’ accounts. Handing over your banking login introduces another service into the security chain. A vulnerability in that service could expose your credentials or allow your account to be misused. And as Bank of America reportedly pointed out: “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.” That’s the bank’s stated position, not a universal ruling on consumers’ legal rights. Still, it’s a warning worth taking seriously. Pros and cons An AI agent with permission to make purchases might find and buy an item at a lower price. But giving an agent access to your bank account also means sharing sensitive banking information with a third party. We’ve seen shared AI chats become searchable online too. Axios reported that many banks allow, or are moving toward allowing, read-only access. This can let a tool analyze transactions without giving it permission to move money. That’s an important boundary, but it doesn’t make the information harmless. An agent that can read bank statements may still disclose them if it’s compromised or manipulated. Preventing transactions and protecting confidentiality are separate security goals. How to keep control of your money For consumers, the practical question is not whether banks have perfectly selfless motives. It’s what access you’re giving away, and what could happen if the agent makes a mistake. Don’t paste banking passwords or security codes into a general-purpose AI assistant. Major banks have explicitly warned customers against sharing their credentials. Use your bank’s approved connection methods rather than giving an agent your login. Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help. Give agents access to as little sensitive information as possible. An assistant comparing publicly advertised savings rates doesn’t need your bank statements. OpenAI recommends limiting agents to the data and credentials they need for the task. Review consequential actions yourself. If an agent asks for confirmation, check exactly what it intends to do and what information it will share. Don’t treat a confirmation prompt as a formality. AI can make it easier to compare financial products and spot opportunities you might otherwise miss. But an assistant that finds a better rate and an agent that can act inside your account are different propositions. Let it help with the homework, but be cautious about handing it the keys. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

items.title: Walk before you run: The digital forensics fundamentals we’re still skipping
items.summary: Authored by Rhys Tooby Originally published in the October 2026 issue of Magnet Unlocked. Want to be the first to see new content? Sign up for our monthly newsletter, Magnet Unlocked. Key takeaways: Automation is a foundational fix for capacity and backlog challenges. Digital forensics labs don’t necessarily need more horsepower. They need to make better use of what they already have. Connected, searchable case data can uncover links that individual investigations miss. Consistently extracting and cross-referencing identifiers such as usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and financial information can surface those connections and give investigators something concrete to pursue. Build the foundation first, then layer AI on top without removing human judgment. AI becomes much more valuable when it sits on clean, organized, connected data and efficient workflows. But neither AI nor automation replaces investigative instinct. Sometimes our instinct is to chase a new and exciting tool, even though there’s proven technology we know how to use and agencies aren’t using properly. It’s been more than eight years since I last worked a case as a police examiner, but I’ve kept close ties to the job. When I catch up with old colleagues, the conversation always lands on AI and how it will change everything. I understand the fear and excitement. But I keep coming back to a less fashionable thought: Don’t run before you can walk. Digital forensics already has proven technology and well-understood techniques . The challenge is making them work consistently at scale. None of it is sci-fi. All of it could be invested in tomorrow. The engine under the bonnet Automation is rarely the sexy tool in the room. It’s the engine under the bonnet (or the hood, depending on which side of the Atlantic you’re reading from). Nobody gets excited about it, but nothing moves without it . Here’s a scene every examiner will recognize. You start imaging a drive and head home at 5:00PM. The image finishes at 6:00PM, or 2:00AM, and then it just sits there. You come in the next day, kick off processing, and wait again. The data is right there. You just can’t look at it yet. When I was honest about my own lab, the truth was uncomfortable. We’d spent serious money on workstations, and I’d estimate they sat idle about 80% of the time. That wasn’t because the work was done. The jobs had finished and the humans had gone home to family, friends and a life outside the lab. That’s how it should be. But the machines don’t need to clock off. They can run 24/7 , moving from acquisition to processing to the next item in the queue while we sleep. That’s the most basic case for automation , and it’s still underused. Why aren’t we doing it? People expect me to say the barrier is fear that automation will replace examiners, or a lack of understanding. Honestly, I think it’s time. Units are fighting backlogs every day . To implement automation properly, you have to put the tools down, step back and rethink how work moves through the lab. When you’re always chasing, there’s never a good moment to stop . That’s exactly why it’s worth making the moment. Every hour spent setting it up comes back as hours you’ll never spend babysitting a progress bar again. And you don’t have to work it out alone. Plenty of agencies around the world have already walked this road, and that experience is there to share. The case we nearly missed Near the end of my policing career, a CSAM investigation was coming to its conclusion. There was a particular username that has been flagged in the chats. An officer went on his lunch break and mentioned it to a colleague, who stopped him because he recognized it. He went back through his own case files and found the same username in an investigation he’d done six months earlier. That link opened up a network of offenders, and more than 160 victims. The breakthrough came from a colleague recognising a username and connecting it to an earlier investigation. It was a powerful reminder of how much valuable intelligence sits across individual cases, and what becomes possible when those connections are made. The identifier had been on our server the whole time. Two investigations, two examiners, two sets of intelligence — each holding a piece of a much bigger picture. What connected them was a conversation between two colleagues over lunch. It stayed with me. Not because anyone had failed to do their job, but because it showed just how important it is to make connections between investigations, intelligence and the people working on them. Sometimes, a single link can change the scale of an investigation — and the number of victims we can identify. This isn’t unique to CSAM . Drugs , fraud, anywhere like-minded offenders talk to each other, the same thing happens. Our intel points us at the investigation in front of us, we work it, and the next team does the same with theirs. Nobody puts two and two together, because nothing in the system is built to. Fix your current workflow, then implement AI People often assume this story is a pitch for AI. What would have caught that link is simple: extracting identifiers and searching across cases. Usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, bank account and card details. Pull them consistently from every case, keep them in one place, and flag when something you’re looking at today has appeared before. It doesn’t have to make the connection for you. It just has to put its hand up and say: this username appeared in another case; someone should take a look. That flag alone gives you a way to triage all the “big data” we keep talking about. Because it’s built on known identifiers, you can trust what it’s telling you. Think about the terabytes sitting on unit servers right now. When we say big data, what are we actually looking at? What have we missed that we don’t even know about? That was my gripe for years, and the answer was never more horsepower or a smarter model. It was getting the basics organized. Updates in Magnet Axiom reflect just that, identifiers from Axiom now feed into the Griffeye Intelligence Database (GID) in Magnet Griffeye . That kind of joint thinking simply didn’t exist when I was in the lab. Get that foundation right and then layer AI on top . Ask it to build out trends and surface patterns. It will be far more useful sitting on clean, connected data than on a pile of disconnected exports. Don’t automate the instinct away There’s a flipside to that lunch-table story. The connection happened because an investigator recognized something. That’s old-school police work, the kind of memory-and-hunch link you’d expect from a Sherlock Holmes story. Automation and AI can do an enormous amount for us. They don’t replace the instinct of someone who has seen other corners of criminality and knows when something doesn’t sit right. The best setup is one where the tools raise the flag, and the investigator brings the judgment. That means keeping relationships and conversations alive across the department, not just inside the lab. Opening the door One more thing has changed since I left the workforce. People joining policing now grew up with smartphones and apps. Digital forensics used to sit behind a closed door, the geeks in the back room who’d sort out that bit of the case. That model doesn’t scale anymore. We used to say 95% of investigations involve digital data. I suspect it’s even higher now. If you’ve got a phone in your pocket, it’s tracking your location. So, the next tipping point is opening; sharing data across the organization and letting more investigators help. Which brings us back to the start. You can’t open the door if what’s behind it is a backlog and a server full of data nobody can search. Walk first. Put the idle hours to work. Build the database. Cross-reference the identifiers. Then we can talk about running .
items.summary_html:
Authored by Rhys Tooby

Originally published in the October 2026 issue of Magnet Unlocked. Want to be the first to see new content? Sign up for our monthly newsletter, Magnet Unlocked.

Key takeaways:
  • Automation is a foundational fix for capacity and backlog challenges.
    Digital forensics labs don’t necessarily need more horsepower. They need to make better use of what they already have.
  • Connected, searchable case data can uncover links that individual investigations miss.
    Consistently extracting and cross-referencing identifiers such as usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and financial information can surface those connections and give investigators something concrete to pursue.
  • Build the foundation first, then layer AI on top without removing human judgment.
    AI becomes much more valuable when it sits on clean, organized, connected data and efficient workflows. But neither AI nor automation replaces investigative instinct.

Sometimes our instinct is to chase a new and exciting tool, even though there’s proven technology we know how to use and agencies aren’t using properly.

It’s been more than eight years since I last worked a case as a police examiner, but I’ve kept close ties to the job. When I catch up with old colleagues, the conversation always lands on AI and how it will change everything. I understand the fear and excitement.

But I keep coming back to a less fashionable thought: Don’t run before you can walk.

Digital forensics already has proven technology and well-understood techniques. The challenge is making them work consistently at scale.

None of it is sci-fi.

All of it could be invested in tomorrow.

The engine under the bonnet

Automation is rarely the sexy tool in the room. It’s the engine under the bonnet (or the hood, depending on which side of the Atlantic you’re reading from). Nobody gets excited about it, but nothing moves without it.

Here’s a scene every examiner will recognize. You start imaging a drive and head home at 5:00PM. The image finishes at 6:00PM, or 2:00AM, and then it just sits there. You come in the next day, kick off processing, and wait again. The data is right there. You just can’t look at it yet.

When I was honest about my own lab, the truth was uncomfortable. We’d spent serious money on workstations, and I’d estimate they sat idle about 80% of the time. That wasn’t because the work was done. The jobs had finished and the humans had gone home to family, friends and a life outside the lab. That’s how it should be. But the machines don’t need to clock off. They can run 24/7, moving from acquisition to processing to the next item in the queue while we sleep. That’s the most basic case for automation, and it’s still underused.

Why aren’t we doing it?

People expect me to say the barrier is fear that automation will replace examiners, or a lack of understanding.

Honestly, I think it’s time.

Units are fighting backlogs every day. To implement automation properly, you have to put the tools down, step back and rethink how work moves through the lab. When you’re always chasing, there’s never a good moment to stop.

That’s exactly why it’s worth making the moment. Every hour spent setting it up comes back as hours you’ll never spend babysitting a progress bar again. And you don’t have to work it out alone. Plenty of agencies around the world have already walked this road, and that experience is there to share.

The case we nearly missed

Near the end of my policing career, a CSAM investigation was coming to its conclusion. There was a particular username that has been flagged in the chats. An officer went on his lunch break and mentioned it to a colleague, who stopped him because he recognized it. He went back through his own case files and found the same username in an investigation he’d done six months earlier.

That link opened up a network of offenders, and more than 160 victims.

The breakthrough came from a colleague recognising a username and connecting it to an earlier investigation. It was a powerful reminder of how much valuable intelligence sits across individual cases, and what becomes possible when those connections are made.

The identifier had been on our server the whole time. Two investigations, two examiners, two sets of intelligence — each holding a piece of a much bigger picture. What connected them was a conversation between two colleagues over lunch.

It stayed with me. Not because anyone had failed to do their job, but because it showed just how important it is to make connections between investigations, intelligence and the people working on them. Sometimes, a single link can change the scale of an investigation — and the number of victims we can identify.

This isn’t unique to CSAM. Drugs, fraud, anywhere like-minded offenders talk to each other, the same thing happens. Our intel points us at the investigation in front of us, we work it, and the next team does the same with theirs.

Nobody puts two and two together, because nothing in the system is built to.

Fix your current workflow, then implement AI

People often assume this story is a pitch for AI.

What would have caught that link is simple: extracting identifiers and searching across cases. Usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, bank account and card details. Pull them consistently from every case, keep them in one place, and flag when something you’re looking at today has appeared before.

It doesn’t have to make the connection for you. It just has to put its hand up and say: this username appeared in another case; someone should take a look. That flag alone gives you a way to triage all the “big data” we keep talking about. Because it’s built on known identifiers, you can trust what it’s telling you.

Think about the terabytes sitting on unit servers right now. When we say big data, what are we actually looking at? What have we missed that we don’t even know about? That was my gripe for years, and the answer was never more horsepower or a smarter model. It was getting the basics organized.

Updates in Magnet Axiom reflect just that, identifiers from Axiom now feed into the Griffeye Intelligence Database (GID) in Magnet Griffeye. That kind of joint thinking simply didn’t exist when I was in the lab.

Get that foundation right and then layer AI on top. Ask it to build out trends and surface patterns. It will be far more useful sitting on clean, connected data than on a pile of disconnected exports.

Don’t automate the instinct away

There’s a flipside to that lunch-table story. The connection happened because an investigator recognized something. That’s old-school police work, the kind of memory-and-hunch link you’d expect from a Sherlock Holmes story.

Automation and AI can do an enormous amount for us. They don’t replace the instinct of someone who has seen other corners of criminality and knows when something doesn’t sit right.

The best setup is one where the tools raise the flag, and the investigator brings the judgment. That means keeping relationships and conversations alive across the department, not just inside the lab.

Opening the door

One more thing has changed since I left the workforce. People joining policing now grew up with smartphones and apps. Digital forensics used to sit behind a closed door, the geeks in the back room who’d sort out that bit of the case.

That model doesn’t scale anymore.

We used to say 95% of investigations involve digital data. I suspect it’s even higher now. If you’ve got a phone in your pocket, it’s tracking your location.

So, the next tipping point is opening; sharing data across the organization and letting more investigators help. Which brings us back to the start. You can’t open the door if what’s behind it is a backlog and a server full of data nobody can search.

Walk first. Put the idle hours to work. Build the database. Cross-reference the identifiers. Then we can talk about running.

items.title: Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys
items.summary: Three malicious Firefox extensions posed as the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys. Whoever holds these secrets controls the wallet and every coin in it. All three listings were live on the Firefox Add-ons store during the research and have since been removed. The fake add-ons copied the names, icons, and marketing text of well-known wallets. Anyone searching the store for a trusted wallet could easily install one by mistake. This is the same trick seen in other fake crypto wallet screens used to trap careless users. Researchers at Socket.dev identified the malware and shared their findings on October 27, 2026. Their team found that the extensions send stolen secrets to subdomains of one command-and-control domain, bonto[.]io. The Phantom copy also carried a hidden loader that could change its behavior after Mozilla approved it. Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget The Phantom listing used lookalike Unicode letters in its name, so it appeared on screen as “Phantom.” It reused Phantom’s real ghost icon and called itself “Official Phantom Wallet (Firefox Update).” The Jupiter copy claimed it was built by Jupiter Exchange. The Bitget copy used the internal name “TabFlow Pro” but showed Bitget branding to users. None of them offered a privacy policy, and all declared that they collect no data. items.title: Hackers Use Fake Court Notices to Deliver XWorm Malware Through Hidden Windows Scripts
items.summary: Attackers are sending fake court notices to organizations in Colombia and using them to install XWorm, a remote access tool that gives criminals full control of an infected PC. The emails look like real legal letters. The attached files are hidden Windows scripts that quietly start the infection. The lure works because few people ignore a message that says a court case needs urgent attention. The emails are written in Spanish and come from Colombian organizations. The file names copy real administrative and legal papers, so a busy employee may open the file without a second thought. Behind that file sits a long chain of hidden steps, similar to the new XWorm infection chain seen last year. Researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs published their findings on GitHub on October 26, 2026. They noted that the campaign targets Colombian organizations. They also found that the final loader matches one used in a separate September 2026 XWorm case linked to the UK, which suggests the attackers are reusing their tools. Hackers Use Fake Court Notices The infection starts with an email that carries a VBScript or JavaScript file. Some files arrive inside ZIP archives, and the second-stage files are downloaded from public file-hosting services such as Filestack and ImageKit. File names like “ACTA_NOTIFICA_TUTELA.js” and “PROCESO DISCIPLINARIO_ RAD_00470032.vbs” are meant to look like real legal papers. Courts in Colombia are a common theme for local criminals, and the same trick appeared in Blind Eagle-linked phishing campaigns that also used fake judicial messages. Once the victim opens the script, it does not show any warning. Instead, it unlocks a hidden PowerShell command. The script is heavily scrambled to avoid detection. The VBScript version uses a custom Base93 decoder and several layers of encryption, while the JavaScript samples use other encryption methods and randomly generated function names. This makes it very hard for antivirus tools to spot the real purpose of the file. The hidden PowerShell code then unpacks two files: a .NET DLL called RSG_UnityApp and the XWorm program itself. PowerShell loads the DLL and passes it the path to RegAsm.exe, a trusted Windows tool, along with the XWorm code. The loader injects XWorm into RegAsm.exe, so the malware runs inside a program that looks normal. Security teams that only watch for unknown files can easily miss this step. What XWorm Can Do and How to Defend Against It After it starts, XWorm reads its hidden settings and contacts its command server. It sends back details about the PC, including the user name, system details, hardware, antivirus status, and whether a webcam is present. Traffic is encrypted with AES-128-ECB, and every message begins with its length followed by a null byte. The researchers saw commands for running shell commands, capturing the screen, managing files, loading plugins, and starting DDoS traffic. XWorm is sold as a service, so many criminals can buy it, and it often ranks high in weekly malware threat rankings . The researchers found three command servers, and the same servers appear in public sandbox records under different sample hashes and mutexes. This points to several separate builds that share the same infrastructure. Arctic Wolf also saw the same loader deliver DCRat in another sample. Defenders should watch for wscript.exe or cscript.exe starting PowerShell, especially with hidden or encoded commands. They should also flag RegAsm.exe when it runs after PowerShell, creates suspended processes, or makes network connections. Checking DNS and firewall logs for the domains and ports below is a quick way to find infected systems. Staff should confirm any court notice through an official channel and never open unexpected script files, which are among the common XWorm delivery methods . items.title: LABScon26 Replay | Keynote: A Sober Analysis of AI Impact
items.summary: In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise. Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation. He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate. This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models About the Author James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group. About LABScon This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

items.title: Claude AI Builds One-Click Chrome and 0-Click Linux Exploit Chains, Bypasses Android Lock Screen
items.summary: Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team says an unreleased Claude research model wrote working exploit chains for Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. The company shared the details in on research post on October 27, 2026. These were lab tests and not real-world incidents. Anthropic reported every bug to the vendor first, and the vendor released fixes. Chrome Falls to a One-Click Chain The Chrome exploit is the most detailed. After a first prompt, Claude wrote a chain that runs code outside the browser sandbox. The test launched the Calculator app on a default Chrome install on macOS within seconds of a page loading. The chain used four bugs. The first corrupted memory in V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine. The second broke out of V8’s memory sandbox, beat ASLR, and took over the renderer process. A race condition in CacheStorage then leaked the layout of the more powerful browser process. A use-after-free bug in FedCM, Chrome’s sign-in feature, finished the escape. Anthropic says Google assigned 62 CVEs, all rated high or critical, including 13 sandbox escapes. All are fixed in Chrome 156. Google’s Chrome 156 release notes from October 20 credit “Xinyang Ge (Anthropic), assisted by Claude” for several fixes, but not for all 62. Safari and Android Bypasses In Safari, Claude broke the same-origin policy, the rule that keeps one website from reading another. The chain started with a use-after-free bug in JavaScriptCore. It then got around WebKit’s Gigacage defense and used a flaw in the sandbox’s IPC mechanism to read history, cookies, and sessions from disk. Anthropic notes this chain never needed code execution. A hostile page could read a signed-in email or bank account. Apple confirmed the report the same day and shipped a fix . The Android case needs physical access. Claude pulled photos and other data from a locked Google Pixel 9 over USB. It did this by linking three flaws that skipped the USB data block, the pairing authorization, and the six-digit code check. A fallback path then sent raw file bytes past a hardcoded block. Anthropic says Google fixed it. Our earlier story on an Android lock screen bypass through Driving Mode shows how often these gaps appear. Windows Crash Bug and the CVE Mismatch Claude also found a remote crash bug in Windows, which Anthropic describes as an out-of-bounds read in the kernel’s QUIC code. It reached the bug by reverse engineering a Windows binary with Ghidra. A few packets could crash and restart a server that answers HTTP/3, and repeating them keeps it down. Anthropic believes several million such servers face the internet. Public records tell a slightly different story. The NVD entry for CVE-2026-33096 names the Windows HTTP.sys driver and not QUIC. It carries a 7.5 score and a fix from April 2026. Rapid7 lists the same details. The NVD entry does not name a finder. Zero-Click Linux Root Access The Linux chain is the most serious. Claude wrote an exploit that gives a remote attacker root access on servers running a multipath TCP listener. It needs no login and no user action. It works in two steps. First, it leaks a kernel pointer to defeat KASLR. Then it reuses the same race condition bug to overwrite a callback pointer and run a shell command. A lost race only fails the handshake and does not crash the machine, so an attacker can try again and again. In the test, the leak took 48 minutes, and the shell took five more. Anthropic ties this to CVE-2026-98432. Its Tenable listing rates it 9.8 and describes an IPv4 TCP use-after-free fix, with no mention of multipath TCP. The link between the two rests on Anthropic’s post. Anthropic says it found so many bugs by running many scanning agents in parallel and checking each finding with a standard process. It also urges teams to scan code at pull request time, and it released a security guidance plugin for Claude Code. Its expanded Cyber Verification Program gives approved security staff access to its strongest models. The same tools can help attackers, so patching speed is critical. Update Chrome to version 156 or later, install current Apple, Android, and Windows updates, and patch Linux kernels. Teams can also read our report on Claude Security’s continuous repository scans and our earlier look at chained Claude.ai flaws . AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Black Duck launches AI agent to fix vulnerabilities as fast as attackers exploit them
items.summary: Application security vendor Black Duck has launched Signal Agentic Fix , a new AI agent designed to shrink the gap between vulnerability discovery and a validated fix reaching production. The agent is the latest addition to Black Duck Signal, the company’s collection of AI agents aimed at removing the human workflow bottlenecks that stop security teams keeping pace with the rising volume of vulnerabilities and exploits. Black Duck says the launch responds to two pressures that AI has intensified for defenders. The first is a swelling remediation backlog, fuelled by the surge in AI-generated code, the higher vulnerability rates found in that code, and a steady flood of new supply chain CVEs. The second is a collapsing time to exploit: attackers are now using AI to chain and weaponise vulnerabilities in hours, while human-led remediation is still typically measured in days or weeks. Scan, triage, fix, validate, submit Signal Agentic Fix automates the full remediation loop: Scan: Black Duck’s deterministic SAST and SCA engines – the same ones behind Polaris, Coverity and Black Duck SCA – identify defects in proprietary code and open source dependencies. Triage: AI assesses severity, reachability and exploitability, filtering out false positives and prioritising the highest-risk issues. Fix: AI generates code fixes for SAST findings, while SCA findings receive dependency upgrade fixes based on Black Duck Security Advisories, informed by the company’s ContextAI knowledge base. Validate: Fixed code is re-scanned and can optionally be run against customer-defined compliance checks and functional tests to confirm no new defects have been introduced. Submit: Every change is routed to a human for review, either via the developer’s AI coding agent or as a pull request in source control. “The differentiator is not that AI can write a fix; it’s whether you can trust it,” said Dipto Chakravarty, Chief Product & Technology Officer at Black Duck. “A harness that pairs deterministic static and software composition analysis with AI-powered triage, fix generation, and validation, plus human-defined guardrails and approval gates is what makes agentic remediation something enterprises can actually trust and deploy.” Two deployment models The agent can work as a security collaborator alongside a developer and their AI coding agent, such as Claude Code. In this mode, Signal Agentic Fix runs the scans and triage, passes findings and fix guidance to the coding agent to implement, then re-scans to validate the result. Because the coding agent makes the change, it is governed by the same hooks and skills a team already uses for code generation. Alternatively, it can sit in the DevOps pipeline, triggering the remediation loop on commits, builds or on demand, generating fixes with a configured LLM and submitting them as pull requests for team approval. For organisations in regulated and safety-critical sectors, Black Duck has built in configurable remediation rules governing what the agent may fix and how, validation rules that let teams apply their own coding and compliance standards and test suites, and mandatory human-in-the-loop approval before anything is merged. Availability Signal Agentic Fix for Claude Code is available in Early Access now, with further coding agent and DevOps pipeline integrations across Polaris, Coverity and Black Duck SCA due in the coming weeks.
