items.title: Node2Shell Vulnerability Actively Exploited in the Wild, CISA Warns
items.summary: CISA has added the Node2Shell flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111497, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Attackers are already sending live exploit traffic at Node.js servers, so teams should patch right away. CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27, 2026. Federal agencies must fix it by November 10, 2026. CISA lists it as an unchecked return value flaw in Google Brotli. It says a remote attacker with no login can use a crafted Brotli stream to corrupt memory, leak data, crash the app, or possibly run code. CISA marks ransomware use as unknown. It also says forensic triage is not required under BOD 26-04. The flaw goes by several names. Researchers call it Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, Broccoli2Shell and Brotli2Shell. Google’s CNA gives it a 9.2 Critical score under CVSS 4.0. The bug is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, and Wiz’s technical write-up covers detection and mitigation for cloud teams. Our own earlier report on the Node2Shell proof of concept covered the first public code execution demo. Things have moved fast since then. Within days, the story went from a lab demo to real attacks. Node2Shell Vulnerability Brotli is a compression format that web servers and clients use to shrink traffic. A Brotli stream is split into blocks, and special switch commands tell the decoder which block type comes next. The trouble starts when a kind of block has only one type declared. A switch in that case is invalid and the decoder should reject it. ELLIO’s research explains that the helper function returned a plain false for this case. It also returned false when the decoder simply ran out of input. Two different problems got the same answer. When the caller hears that more input is needed, it sends more. The decoder keeps leftover bytes in an internal eight-byte buffer. A real shortage drains that buffer on the next chunk. An invalid switch never drains it. The bytes keep piling up, and past the eighth byte the writes land outside the buffer. Because the write uses a signed 32-bit offset, an attacker can pick a spot within roughly 2 GB and copy 16 bytes of their own data there. The fix is upstream commit 0ed4268a. It makes the helper return a real error code, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH with value -17, so bad streams stop at once. The bug has been in Brotli since version 1.0.3 in March 2018. ELLIO says the fix sat in the public master branch from February 2026 with no release or advisory for about eight months. Who Is Affected Node.js 22.x, 24.x and 26.x are hit, and so are the end-of-life 20.x, 23.x and 25.x lines. The old lines will get no fix. Fixed Node.js versions are 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Google fixed Brotli in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. A bare Node.js server does not unpack a Brotli body just because it arrives. Something has to pass the bytes to the decoder. ELLIO describes three common paths. The first is an inbound request with Content-Encoding set to br. Express 5 with express.json() or express.raw(), body-parser 2 and Koa with @koa/bodyparser all unpack it before any route code runs. The second is an outbound fetch. Built-in fetch(), axios, got, and SuperAgent will decode a hostile server’s reply, so link previews, webhooks, and crawlers are all at risk. The third is any direct node:zlib call on client data. The problem reaches well past Node.js. Bun before 1.4.4 is affected, and so are the Python packages Brotli and brotlicffi, which need 1.2.1 and 1.2.1.0. Envoy, the Ruby brotli gem, and many Linux distributions are also on the list. The CIS advisory says the flaw sits in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. Tenable’s FAQ lists affected products in one place. One trap is worth knowing. Node.js cherry-picked the fix without changing the bundled version string. So process.versions.brotli shows 1.2.0 on both patched and unpatched builds. Check the Node.js release number instead. Imperva’s Red Team showed the first working exploit on October 22. They ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, using both fetch() and Express 5 request bodies. Their write-up, Node2Shell: From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution , says version 24.22.1 rejected the same input. ELLIO then repeated the attack on x86-64. It got a shell on four targets running the same build. These were a plain node:http server, the official node:24.22.0-slim image running as root, Express 5.3.0, and Koa 3. Each shell ran as the service’s own account. The lab found that official Node.js builds are non-PIE, so the binary loads at the same address every time. Address space layout randomization still shuffles the heap and stacks, so an attacker has to guess. With ASLR on, a shell appeared at around attempt 5. With ASLR off, 60 attempts gave no hit. Turning it off does not help. Two target-specific values decide success. One is the number of the accepted socket, which the shell uses for input and output. The other is a memory offset tied to one exact Node.js build. The offset for 24.22.0 gave nothing against 22.23.3 or 26.12.0 in 10,000 tries. That limits attackers to waves aimed at one popular build at a time. Scanning began first. A checker calling itself node2shell-check/1.0 hit ELLIO’s sensors from AS44620. It sent 20 Brotli bodies in two bursts to find hosts that decompress Brotli at all. None carried the real trigger. This looked like list building ahead of an attack. Exploit traffic followed on October 26 at 15:08 UTC. ELLIO saw a single 23,069,983-byte request with SHA-256 7fcbdaaecd4419e2930927844f3b772668204737a4e7602a2290c991c93c5c4b. It came from 94.154.43.7, an address ELLIO rates as malicious with high confidence. The address was first seen in December 2025 and was active on 47 of the last 90 days. It has been tied to PHP2Shell exploitation, Palo Alto GlobalProtect and FortiOS SSL VPN probing, and Kubernetes scanning. The request targets only Node.js v24.22.0 on x86-64. The delivery layer copies public exploit code. The ROP chain, which takes over the process, is original. It plants /bin/sh in its own data and calls Node’s execvp from there. It does not use the string already inside Node, as both public chains do. ELLIO tested it against a clean vulnerable target and got zero shells in 50 attempts. The chain crashed the process instead. ELLIO thinks this was a first try fired before the operator tested the last step. It warns that the operator looks focused on mass exploitation. Teams that remember React2Shell will see the same pattern of fast public code followed by quick scanning. Microsoft documented that earlier flaw in its React2Shell defense guide . Failed attempts are not harmless. ELLIO saw that most of its 400 Express attempts crashed the worker instead of giving a shell. A crash can write a core dump, and that dump may hold session cookies, tokens and keys from other visitors. On a stock Ubuntu host, systemd-coredump saves these files in /var/lib/systemd/coredump. Containers usually write nothing, so the harm there is only downtime. Some other decoders hang quietly instead. Python Brotli 1.2.0, brotlicffi 1.2.0.0, the PHP streaming API and the Ruby gem all return nothing and never finish, and the PHP case spins at 100% CPU. Patch first. Move Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, and update Bun, Python packages, Envoy, and any distro Brotli library. Debian users should look for DLA-4855-1 or DSA-6582-1. Alpine users need brotli 1.2.1-r0, or 1.1.1-r0 on 3.21. Leave the old 20.x, 23.x and 25.x lines behind, since they will never be fixed. A Node.js upgrade only fixes the copied Node bundles. Tools with their own copy, like bun build –compile executables, DuckDB, and PHP extensions, need separate updates. Rebuild images, refresh lockfiles, and restart processes. A Dockerfile that pins 24.22.0 keeps shipping the bad build until someone edits that line. Check staging, CI, serverless, and developer laptops too. Until patching is done, block inbound Content-Encoding: br where you can. Also watch logs for large Brotli POST bodies, repeated worker crashes, and the IP and hash above. Limit who can read core dumps, and shorten how long you keep them. Federal teams face the November 10 deadline, but every other team should treat that date as a ceiling and not a goal. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

CISA has added the Node2Shell flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111497, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Attackers are already sending live exploit traffic at Node.js servers, so teams should patch right away.

CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27, 2026. Federal agencies must fix it by November 10, 2026. CISA lists it as an unchecked return value flaw in Google Brotli. It says a remote attacker with no login can use a crafted Brotli stream to corrupt memory, leak data, crash the app, or possibly run code. CISA marks ransomware use as unknown. It also says forensic triage is not required under BOD 26-04.

The flaw goes by several names. Researchers call it Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, Broccoli2Shell and Brotli2Shell. Google’s CNA gives it a 9.2 Critical score under CVSS 4.0. The bug is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, and Wiz’s technical write-up covers detection and mitigation for cloud teams.

Our own earlier report on the Node2Shell proof of concept covered the first public code execution demo. Things have moved fast since then. Within days, the story went from a lab demo to real attacks.

Node2Shell Vulnerability

Brotli is a compression format that web servers and clients use to shrink traffic. A Brotli stream is split into blocks, and special switch commands tell the decoder which block type comes next. The trouble starts when a kind of block has only one type declared.

A switch in that case is invalid and the decoder should reject it. ELLIO’s research explains that the helper function returned a plain false for this case. It also returned false when the decoder simply ran out of input. Two different problems got the same answer.

When the caller hears that more input is needed, it sends more. The decoder keeps leftover bytes in an internal eight-byte buffer. A real shortage drains that buffer on the next chunk. An invalid switch never drains it. The bytes keep piling up, and past the eighth byte the writes land outside the buffer. Because the write uses a signed 32-bit offset, an attacker can pick a spot within roughly 2 GB and copy 16 bytes of their own data there.

The fix is upstream commit 0ed4268a. It makes the helper return a real error code, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH with value -17, so bad streams stop at once. The bug has been in Brotli since version 1.0.3 in March 2018. ELLIO says the fix sat in the public master branch from February 2026 with no release or advisory for about eight months.

Who Is Affected

Node.js 22.x, 24.x and 26.x are hit, and so are the end-of-life 20.x, 23.x and 25.x lines. The old lines will get no fix. Fixed Node.js versions are 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Google fixed Brotli in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1.

A bare Node.js server does not unpack a Brotli body just because it arrives. Something has to pass the bytes to the decoder. ELLIO describes three common paths. The first is an inbound request with Content-Encoding set to br. Express 5 with express.json() or express.raw(), body-parser 2 and Koa with @koa/bodyparser all unpack it before any route code runs.

The second is an outbound fetch. Built-in fetch(), axios, got, and SuperAgent will decode a hostile server’s reply, so link previews, webhooks, and crawlers are all at risk. The third is any direct node:zlib call on client data.

The problem reaches well past Node.js. Bun before 1.4.4 is affected, and so are the Python packages Brotli and brotlicffi, which need 1.2.1 and 1.2.1.0. Envoy, the Ruby brotli gem, and many Linux distributions are also on the list. The CIS advisory says the flaw sits in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. Tenable’s FAQ lists affected products in one place.

One trap is worth knowing. Node.js cherry-picked the fix without changing the bundled version string. So process.versions.brotli shows 1.2.0 on both patched and unpatched builds. Check the Node.js release number instead.

Imperva’s Red Team showed the first working exploit on October 22. They ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, using both fetch() and Express 5 request bodies. Their write-up, Node2Shell: From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution, says version 24.22.1 rejected the same input.

ELLIO then repeated the attack on x86-64. It got a shell on four targets running the same build. These were a plain node:http server, the official node:24.22.0-slim image running as root, Express 5.3.0, and Koa 3. Each shell ran as the service’s own account.

The lab found that official Node.js builds are non-PIE, so the binary loads at the same address every time. Address space layout randomization still shuffles the heap and stacks, so an attacker has to guess. With ASLR on, a shell appeared at around attempt 5. With ASLR off, 60 attempts gave no hit. Turning it off does not help.

Two target-specific values decide success. One is the number of the accepted socket, which the shell uses for input and output. The other is a memory offset tied to one exact Node.js build. The offset for 24.22.0 gave nothing against 22.23.3 or 26.12.0 in 10,000 tries. That limits attackers to waves aimed at one popular build at a time.

Scanning began first. A checker calling itself node2shell-check/1.0 hit ELLIO’s sensors from AS44620. It sent 20 Brotli bodies in two bursts to find hosts that decompress Brotli at all. None carried the real trigger. This looked like list building ahead of an attack.

Exploit traffic followed on October 26 at 15:08 UTC. ELLIO saw a single 23,069,983-byte request with SHA-256 7fcbdaaecd4419e2930927844f3b772668204737a4e7602a2290c991c93c5c4b. It came from 94.154.43.7, an address ELLIO rates as malicious with high confidence.

The address was first seen in December 2025 and was active on 47 of the last 90 days. It has been tied to PHP2Shell exploitation, Palo Alto GlobalProtect and FortiOS SSL VPN probing, and Kubernetes scanning. The request targets only Node.js v24.22.0 on x86-64.

The delivery layer copies public exploit code. The ROP chain, which takes over the process, is original. It plants /bin/sh in its own data and calls Node’s execvp from there. It does not use the string already inside Node, as both public chains do.

ELLIO tested it against a clean vulnerable target and got zero shells in 50 attempts. The chain crashed the process instead. ELLIO thinks this was a first try fired before the operator tested the last step. It warns that the operator looks focused on mass exploitation. Teams that remember React2Shell will see the same pattern of fast public code followed by quick scanning. Microsoft documented that earlier flaw in its React2Shell defense guide.

Failed attempts are not harmless. ELLIO saw that most of its 400 Express attempts crashed the worker instead of giving a shell. A crash can write a core dump, and that dump may hold session cookies, tokens and keys from other visitors.

On a stock Ubuntu host, systemd-coredump saves these files in /var/lib/systemd/coredump. Containers usually write nothing, so the harm there is only downtime. Some other decoders hang quietly instead. Python Brotli 1.2.0, brotlicffi 1.2.0.0, the PHP streaming API and the Ruby gem all return nothing and never finish, and the PHP case spins at 100% CPU.

Patch first. Move Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, and update Bun, Python packages, Envoy, and any distro Brotli library. Debian users should look for DLA-4855-1 or DSA-6582-1. Alpine users need brotli 1.2.1-r0, or 1.1.1-r0 on 3.21. Leave the old 20.x, 23.x and 25.x lines behind, since they will never be fixed.

A Node.js upgrade only fixes the copied Node bundles. Tools with their own copy, like bun build –compile executables, DuckDB, and PHP extensions, need separate updates. Rebuild images, refresh lockfiles, and restart processes.

A Dockerfile that pins 24.22.0 keeps shipping the bad build until someone edits that line. Check staging, CI, serverless, and developer laptops too.

Until patching is done, block inbound Content-Encoding: br where you can. Also watch logs for large Brotli POST bodies, repeated worker crashes, and the IP and hash above. Limit who can read core dumps, and shorten how long you keep them. Federal teams face the November 10 deadline, but every other team should treat that date as a ceiling and not a goal.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Veeam Patches Critical Backup & Replication Authorization Bypass Vulnerability
items.summary: Veeam released security fixes for a critical authorization bypass vulnerability in Veeam Backup & Replication that lets an attacker without login credentials bypass access checks on the CDP Coordinator Service . Tracked as CVE-2026-108142, the flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.1 and affects both Windows-based deployments and the Veeam Software Appliance. The company disclosed the issue on October 27, 2026, in its security advisory KB4948 . The advisory also covers two medium-severity file-write vulnerabilities in Backup & Replication and a high-severity local privilege escalation flaw in Veeam Agent for Linux. HackerOne reported all four issues. CVE-2026-108142 affects Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.1.18 and earlier builds in the 13.1 branch, along with 13.0.2.29 and earlier builds in the 13.0 branch. Veeam identifies version 12.x as unaffected by this issue. The flaw concerns authorization, the checks that decide which actions a caller can perform. Veeam says an unauthenticated attacker can bypass those checks on the CDP Coordinator Service. However, the advisory does not describe the attack sequence or state that the vulnerability enables remote code execution . It also does not report active exploitation. Veeam Patches Backup & Replication Vulnerability Veeam lists the first fixed releases as Backup & Replication 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.57, and Backup & Replication 13.0.3, build 13.0.3.63. Administrators should match their installed version against these build numbers rather than checking only the main product version. The update also addresses CVE-2026-108140 and CVE-2026-108141, each rated medium severity with a CVSS v4.0 score of 5.9. Both require an authenticated user with the Restore Operator role who also controls the contents of a backed-up network-attached storage (NAS) share. Under those conditions, an attacker can use relative path traversal to write attacker-controlled files to an arbitrary path on the backup server. In simple terms, the file path can escape its intended folder. Veeam lists the same affected Backup & Replication builds and fixed releases for both vulnerabilities. The separate Linux issue, CVE-2026-105477, has a high-severity score of 7.3. It allows local privilege escalation and affects only Veeam Agent for Linux installations managed by Backup & Replication. Affected releases include 13.1.1.4 and earlier 13.1 builds. The fix starts with version 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11. Cyber Security News previously reported attackers exploiting CVE-2024-40711 in Veeam to deploy Frag ransomware , highlighting backup security risks, though this separate vulnerability does not confirm exploitation of the newly disclosed authorization bypass. The publication also reported Veeam’s October security update for version 12.3.2 , noting that different product branches may require different patches. Administrators can check their installed Backup & Replication build through Help > About in the console. Veeam’s release information page provides update guidance. The company warns that attackers may study released patches to find ways into unpatched systems, making timely installation important across affected backup servers and managed Linux agents. items.title: Chrome and Firefox updates fix serious security flaws. Install them now
items.summary: On October 27, Google issued a new Stable channel update for Chrome. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 156.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and 156.0.8078.73 for Linux . The update includes 52 security fixes, including four rated Critical. On the same day, Mozilla issued Security Advisory 2026-118 , which fixes 167 vulnerabilities. Firefox 159 also introduces several new features. Both updates will roll out over the coming days and weeks. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, manually updating is easy. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome version 156.0.8078.74 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . How to update Firefox To update Firefox, open the browser and click the menu button at the right side of the Firefox toolbar, then go to Help and select About Firefox . The About Mozilla Firefox window will open. Firefox will automatically check for updates. If one is available, it will be downloaded. Once done, you’ll be prompted to click Relaunch . After Firefox restarts, it will be up to date. After the update, the version should be 159.0 or later Technical details These Chrome and Firefox updates address a familiar problem: browser code mishandling memory while processing web content. Both releases fix use-after-free vulnerabilities, including flaws in page layout, JavaScript processing, and SVG graphics. A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code. There’s another connection between these updates: both Google and Mozilla credit OpenAI Codex Security with finding bugs fixed in these releases. AI can help security teams examine browser code for weaknesses, alongside human code reviews and automated tests that check how software handles unexpected inputs. Mozilla’s collaboration with Anthropic shows how AI-discovered findings can lead to fixes: researchers validated vulnerabilities before reporting them, giving Mozilla’s team reproducible bugs to investigate, repair, and deliver to users. items.title: Hackers Compromise Camera Management Software to Deploy Malware on Windows Computers
items.summary: Hackers have compromised camera management software to deploy malware on Windows computers, using a legitimate Microsoft program to run malicious code and maintain access. The activity shows how software used to manage surveillance systems can become an entry point into business networks. The incidents followed a similar pattern: attackers gained access through the camera application, deployed a suspected reverse shell, and used DLL sideloading to contact an outside server. Like earlier cases involving abuse of monitoring tools , the activity highlights risks surrounding software trusted for routine operations. Researchers from Huntress identified the malware activity across several customer environments during September and October 2026. In their October 27 investigation, Harlan Carvey and Lindsey O’Donnell-Welch described a handful of incidents linked to compromised camera management software, while noting important gaps in understanding the initial break-in. Hackers Compromise Camera Management Software The affected application lacked embedded file version information, preventing researchers from confirming its full product name or developer. They also could not locate application logs, leaving the exact method used to compromise the software unresolved. The report does not identify a specific vulnerability or CVE. Investigators found strings connecting the executable to a domain associated with Korean company 3R Global. A camera management package available through another website contained matching strings. However, Huntress stressed that these overlaps did not establish the vendor’s identity or prove where affected customers obtained their software. After gaining access, attackers placed an executable inside a user’s application data directory. Its command line specified a remote address, a connection port, and authentication values. Combined with its location in a writable folder, these details led researchers to assess the program as a reverse shell. The attackers then copied Windows Parental Control Monitor into another application data folder. Huntress verified that this executable was a genuine Microsoft file, but its unusual location exposed the abuse. Similar VLC and VMware sideloading cases demonstrate why a trusted executable alone cannot establish that nearby libraries are safe. Here, the Microsoft program loaded malicious DLLs placed alongside it. The libraries resembled legitimate zlib compression components but had been modified to periodically contact a command-and-control server. This technique, called DLL sideloading, lets attackers execute their code through an otherwise legitimate application. The distinction matters because the executable itself was not the malicious payload. Its role was to load attacker-controlled libraries from the surrounding folder. Checking the Microsoft file’s identity without examining its location, loaded DLLs, parent process, and network activity would leave out the evidence that connected an apparently normal Windows component to the wider infection chain. Persistence, Detection, and Defensive Priorities Attackers maintained access by adding the relocated Microsoft executable to the user’s Run registry key. Windows would then launch it whenever that user signed in, restarting the loading chain. Every investigated incident involved communication with the same command-and-control IP address listed below. For defenders, the most useful signal is the connected sequence of events rather than any single filename. Camera software launching an unexpected executable, followed by a Microsoft component running from a writable folder and making unusual outbound connections, warrants investigation. Huntress specifically recommends examining that process chain. Organizations should inventory camera management applications, restrict access, and monitor their network activity. Earlier EggStreme DLL sideloading attacks also abused a Windows executable from an application data folder, reinforcing the value of checking execution locations. Where practical, Huntress recommends application controls that block unapproved executables and DLLs in user-writable directories. The investigation also leaves limits on what organizations can conclude. Huntress did not establish how the initial camera software compromise occurred, and the available evidence does not justify describing this as a confirmed vendor supply-chain breach. The immediate lesson is narrower: camera management applications need the same endpoint oversight as other business software, rather than being overlooked entirely. https://people.well.com/user/doctorow/metacrap.htm

This compounding error rate only increases as you add more and more bots, so every time you add a new specialized bot to decrease the error rate in its area of specialization, you increase the overall error rate of the system by adding more complexity to it.

For example, Microsoft has repeatedly announced that it will modify Windows to eliminate all forms of PC-side privacy and confidentiality, sending a continuous stream of screenshots to Microsoft's cloud servers so that your Microsoft "agent" can access your private data on Microsoft's cloud:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/06/1000x-liability/#graceful-failure-modes

This is the same demand that the Semantic Web people made in the early oughts, and it has the same problems. The Semantic Web people operated on the assumption that there were freestanding, objectively correct ways of describing things and that everyone who put information on the web would eventually come to see that adopting these correct semantics was to everyone's advantage.

In reality, these semantic differences are the expression of real, serious, unresolvable philosophical, technical, moral and political arguments. The reason that some media outlets won't describe transwomen as women isn't because they lack an appreciation of objectively correct semantic classifications – it's because they're bigots. That's the same reason "race realists" insist that there is a biological category called "race," that exists despite everything computational genomics has proved:

https://pluralistic.net/2020/08/16/combat-wheelchairs/#race-realism

In my book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI, I predicted that a similar dynamic would play out when it came to agentic AI and websites. The reason websites are so inhospitable to bots is that ecommerce sites don't want to be legible to automated tools:

https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374621568/thereversecentaursguidetolifeafterai/

Ecommerce websites deploy a wide range of sleazy tactics to raise prices, including surveillance pricing:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/07/gouged/#aeropain

They use market power to rig whole categories, forcing prices up:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/15/enshittipedia/

Multiple law-enforcers, Republic and Democrat, state and federal, have sued companies for "drip pricing" and "junk fees" that make it impossible to know what the actual price is until you've spent a long-ass time going through the purchase process:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/07/drip-drip-drip/#drip-off

Surveillance pricing, drip pricing, junk fees, price fixing and "most favored nation" deals are the source of all the growth in profitability by the economy's largest, most important firms. https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities

Cheating is so profitable that it's cheaper for firms to buy off regulators and pay fines than it is for them to stop criming. https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/18/surprise/#wow-signal

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/21/cod-marxism/#wannamaker-slain

https://gizmodo.com/online-shopping-platforms-turn-against-third-party-ai-agents-2000831298

items.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting New Oracle EBS RCE Vulnerability
items.summary: Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026. However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the activity was detected. Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the flaw carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. Horizon3.ai discovered the issue and reported it to Oracle on July 24. Oracle fixed it on October 20 through its October Critical Patch Update . Although initially reported privately as a zero-day, it was a publicly disclosed, patched vulnerability when Defused observed the probes. Oracle EBS 0-Day Vulnerability The weakness affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library in EBS versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. It requires network access over HTTP or HTTPS but needs neither valid credentials nor user interaction. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its report on Oracle’s October security update . According to Horizon3.ai’s technical advisory , the vulnerable Thin Client Framework servlet is reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer . A crafted request can trigger SQL injection, allowing an attacker to send database commands as the powerful APPS database user. That access can then be chained into operating system command execution under the EBS application account. The impact extends beyond database access. Successful exploitation could expose or alter financial, payroll, human resources, and purchasing records accessible to APPS. Commands run with the application account’s permissions, rather than automatically granting full administrative control over the host. Defused described the October 27 traffic as “exploratory exploits” against its Oracle EBS decoys. According to reports, no other public reports of exploitation had surfaced. This supports reporting active exploit attempts, but not confirmed breaches, stolen data, or a widespread campaign. Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27. The bug was recently disclosed by @Horizon3ai and… pic.twitter.com/fY9sEbnLRg — Defused (@DefusedCyber) October 27, 2026 The distinction matters because Oracle EBS has faced damaging attacks before. Cyber Security News documented Cl0p exploitation of a separate Oracle EBS zero-day , CVE-2025-61882. That earlier campaign should not be confused with the newly observed TCF servlet probes. Administrators should apply the relevant October patches promptly. Until then, Horizon3.ai recommends removing the servlet from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restricting web access to trusted networks. The default URL firewall permits the endpoint, making configuration checks important. Defenders should review unauthenticated POST requests invoking GanttDataServer , especially when followed by database queries. Other warning signs include unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account launching /bin/sh through Concurrent Manager. Access restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026.

However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the activity was detected.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the flaw carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. Horizon3.ai discovered the issue and reported it to Oracle on July 24. Oracle fixed it on October 20 through its October Critical Patch Update. Although initially reported privately as a zero-day, it was a publicly disclosed, patched vulnerability when Defused observed the probes.

Oracle EBS 0-Day Vulnerability

The weakness affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library in EBS versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. It requires network access over HTTP or HTTPS but needs neither valid credentials nor user interaction. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its report on Oracle’s October security update.

According to Horizon3.ai’s technical advisory, the vulnerable Thin Client Framework servlet is reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer. A crafted request can trigger SQL injection, allowing an attacker to send database commands as the powerful APPS database user. That access can then be chained into operating system command execution under the EBS application account.

The impact extends beyond database access. Successful exploitation could expose or alter financial, payroll, human resources, and purchasing records accessible to APPS. Commands run with the application account’s permissions, rather than automatically granting full administrative control over the host.

Defused described the October 27 traffic as “exploratory exploits” against its Oracle EBS decoys. According to reports, no other public reports of exploitation had surfaced. This supports reporting active exploit attempts, but not confirmed breaches, stolen data, or a widespread campaign.

Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27.

The bug was recently disclosed by @Horizon3ai and… pic.twitter.com/fY9sEbnLRg

— Defused (@DefusedCyber) October 27, 2026

The distinction matters because Oracle EBS has faced damaging attacks before. Cyber Security News documented Cl0p exploitation of a separate Oracle EBS zero-day, CVE-2025-61882. That earlier campaign should not be confused with the newly observed TCF servlet probes.

Administrators should apply the relevant October patches promptly. Until then, Horizon3.ai recommends removing the servlet from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restricting web access to trusted networks. The default URL firewall permits the endpoint, making configuration checks important.

Defenders should review unauthenticated POST requests invoking GanttDataServer, especially when followed by database queries. Other warning signs include unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account launching /bin/sh through Concurrent Manager. Access restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

items.title: FortiBleed 2.0 Reveals Thousands of Fortinet VPN and Active Directory Credentials in Exposed Configurations
items.summary: FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services, and internal identity systems. The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers. The material also includes administrator logins, email-server passwords, and high-availability cluster secrets. These figures reflect records, not unique users, confirmed physical devices, or credentials that still work today. Despite its name, FortiBleed 2.0 is a follow-up investigation based on recently obtained files, not a newly disclosed vulnerability. Most files are dated February 20, 2026, while 31 are undated, leaving the timing of initial access and configuration theft unconfirmed. FortiBleed 2.0 Exposes Fortinet VPN and AD Credentials Compared with the first dataset, researchers identified 924 additional host identifiers and 975 domain labels absent from the earlier collection. Overview of Hudson Rock’s free FortiBleed lookup portal However, domain labels can belong to service providers, registration contacts, or account holders. They should not be read as 975 newly compromised companies. The findings expand earlier FortiBleed credential exposure coverage by revealing accounts and services behind perimeter logins. The associated toolchain extracts firewall configurations, recovers stored secrets, and attempts further access. Its parsing workflow collects local users, administrator entries, LDAP connections, cluster settings, and email credentials. Some stored FortiOS ENC values can be recovered offline when configurations use the system-default encryption key. Recovery depends on the software version, settings, and available material. Cavalier Exposes 54 Credential Records Across Two Hosts Exposed local-user passwords may support VPN access, but account status, access rules, reachability, and multifactor authentication determine whether login succeeds. Hudson Rock’s analysis identified 7,437 disabled local-user records containing cleartext data. Empty MFA fields do not necessarily indicate missing MFA, as external authentication systems may enforce it. LDAP bind credentials deserve close attention because they connect FortiGate appliances to directory services. An account with excessive rights could increase the impact of a breach. Ordinary LDAP query access, however, does not automatically grant domain-administrator privileges. Earlier reporting on FortiGate configuration theft highlights this route toward internal access. Cavalier’s Breach Data Fortinet’s response guidance calls for terminating administrator and VPN sessions, resetting credentials, enforcing MFA, updating firmware, and restricting management access. Security teams should compare current settings with a trusted configuration and examine firewall and domain-controller logs for unexpected activity. The configuration findings also call for reviewing LDAP bind passwords, cluster secrets, and email-server credentials. Investigators should verify ownership of recurring administrator accounts such as fgtsecure and forticloud-sync before treating them as unauthorized. Account names alone do not establish malicious activity. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services, and internal identity systems.

The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers.

The material also includes administrator logins, email-server passwords, and high-availability cluster secrets. These figures reflect records, not unique users, confirmed physical devices, or credentials that still work today.

Despite its name, FortiBleed 2.0 is a follow-up investigation based on recently obtained files, not a newly disclosed vulnerability. Most files are dated February 20, 2026, while 31 are undated, leaving the timing of initial access and configuration theft unconfirmed.

FortiBleed 2.0 Exposes Fortinet VPN and AD Credentials

Compared with the first dataset, researchers identified 924 additional host identifiers and 975 domain labels absent from the earlier collection.

Overview of Hudson Rock’s free FortiBleed lookup portal

However, domain labels can belong to service providers, registration contacts, or account holders. They should not be read as 975 newly compromised companies. The findings expand earlier FortiBleed credential exposure coverage by revealing accounts and services behind perimeter logins.

The associated toolchain extracts firewall configurations, recovers stored secrets, and attempts further access. Its parsing workflow collects local users, administrator entries, LDAP connections, cluster settings, and email credentials.

Some stored FortiOS ENC values can be recovered offline when configurations use the system-default encryption key. Recovery depends on the software version, settings, and available material.

Cavalier Exposes 54 Credential Records Across Two Hosts

Exposed local-user passwords may support VPN access, but account status, access rules, reachability, and multifactor authentication determine whether login succeeds.

Hudson Rock’s analysis identified 7,437 disabled local-user records containing cleartext data. Empty MFA fields do not necessarily indicate missing MFA, as external authentication systems may enforce it.

LDAP bind credentials deserve close attention because they connect FortiGate appliances to directory services. An account with excessive rights could increase the impact of a breach.

Ordinary LDAP query access, however, does not automatically grant domain-administrator privileges. Earlier reporting on FortiGate configuration theft highlights this route toward internal access.

Cavalier’s Breach Data

Fortinet’s response guidance calls for terminating administrator and VPN sessions, resetting credentials, enforcing MFA, updating firmware, and restricting management access.

Security teams should compare current settings with a trusted configuration and examine firewall and domain-controller logs for unexpected activity. The configuration findings also call for reviewing LDAP bind passwords, cluster secrets, and email-server credentials.

Investigators should verify ownership of recurring administrator accounts such as fgtsecure and forticloud-sync before treating them as unauthorized. Account names alone do not establish malicious activity.

items.title: Your security tool flagged the sensitive file. Can anyone still read it?
items.summary: Part 1 split AI agents into two kinds and looked at the controls BigID and Varonis are building for them. Part 2 covered what protecting the data does for each kind, and where it stops. This part is about how to tell, during an evaluation, which kind of tool you’re actually looking at. DLP, DSPM, and data-centric protection do different jobs A lot of tools get called data security, and buyers often assume they overlap more than they do. Data loss prevention (DLP) watches the ways data leaves your company, like email, web uploads, and USB drives, and blocks or flags what looks sensitive. Data security posture management (DSPM) scans where data is stored, classifies it, and flags exposure, such as a folder anyone in the company can open. Both find data and watch what happens to it, and that’s valuable. Data-centric protection acts on the data once it’s found. It encrypts, masks, redacts, quarantines, or deletes it, so the file is protected without waiting on someone to respond to an alert. One doesn’t replace the other. Going by their own published materials, neither BigID nor Varonis encrypts data natively. BigID orchestrates encryption through separate tools, and Varonis’s core platform discovers, classifies, and monitors without native encryption. Both do a good job of showing where sensitive data lives and who or what touched it, and both do things PK Protect doesn’t, including DLP and governing agent access. Neither is designed to make a file unreadable to an agent that reached it without permission. Five questions to ask in any DSPM or DLP evaluation 1 When the tool flags that someone or something reached a sensitive file it shouldn’t have, what happens to the file? If the answer is that an alert fires, ask what that person or agent can do with the contents before someone acts on the alert. 2 Is encryption built into the platform, or does it come from a separate tool? A separate tool is one more thing to buy, deploy, and keep in sync, and any gap between discovery and protection leaves classified data unprotected. 3 Does the protection stay with the file when the file moves? Files get copied and exported to places nobody planned for, and they’re only protected there if the protection is part of the file. 4 Does it cover mainframe and on-prem systems, or only cloud and SaaS? Many DSPM tools started in the cloud. If your sensitive data is on z/OS, IBM i, or file servers in your own data center, ask about those specifically. 5 How does it handle each kind of AI agent as their numbers grow? For assistants working on a person’s behalf, ask how it helps you cut down what each person can reach, since the assistant can reach the same things. For agents with their own identity, ask whether each new one has to be found and given permissions before it’s covered, or whether the data stays unreadable to it either way. Why the first question matters A readable file in the wrong hands is expensive. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report put the average U.S. breach at $10.22 million. The number of identities that could reach that file is growing too. Machine identities now outnumber human ones about 109 to 1, and 40% of them can reach company data. A DSPM or DLP tool can flag a file and still leave it readable to whatever copies it. Changing that takes something that protects the data itself. Where PK Protect fits PK Protect is built for that part of the problem. It finds sensitive data on endpoints, in the cloud, in Microsoft 365, and on z/OS and IBM i, and classifies it under one classification policy. From there, your team can encrypt, mask, redact, quarantine, or delete what it finds. Protection stays on the file after it moves, so an agent running under its own identity can’t read an encrypted file without access to the key. For assistants working on a person’s behalf, cleaning up overexposed data and masking or redacting values people don’t need limits what those assistants can surface. Format-preserving encryption keeps protected data usable for the systems that depend on it. To be clear about the limits, PK Protect won’t stop a file transfer while it’s happening, it won’t tell you what your agents are doing, and it won’t stop an assistant from reading what its user is allowed to read. If you’d like to see what sensitive data is in your environment today and what it would take to protect it, request an assessment . Sources PKWARE vs. BigID and PKWARE vs. Varonis , PKWARE comparison pages drawn from each company’s published materials. Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 , IBM. 2026 Identity Security Landscape , Palo Alto Networks.

items.title: Waiting on a Node.js Upgrade? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
items.summary: Executive Summary Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix. Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line. Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods. Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify. Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes. It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first. Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix. These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change. Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF. Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve* , and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters. Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms. Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control. Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions. Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses. Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder. After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself. Node.js 3rd-party Mitigation and Compensating Controls The table below lists the rules and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-111497 and the related Node.js CVEs, ready to copy into your console. Layer Vendor Control CVEs How it helps Edge (WAF) Cloudflare Managed rule 8f252673b6 9d47afb21f8 8acca706f3c, Brotli – Request Content-Encoding CVE-2026-111497 Matches inbound requests that declare Content-Encoding: br. It ships in Log mode, so set it to Block. Network (IPS) FortiGate IPS signature 62703 CVE-2026-111497 Blocks the crafted request inline before it reaches the decoder. Network (IPS) Check Point Advisory CPAI-2026-15802 CVE-2026-111497 Blocks the exploit attempt at the gateway. Host (EDR) CrowdStrike Suspicious Process Prevention (Linux, macOS, Windows) CVE-2026-111497, 106070, 106071, 106073 Blocks a Node.js process that spawns shells, downloaders, or newly written binaries after exploitation. items.summary_html:
Executive Summary

Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix.

Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js

Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first.

Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations

Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix.

These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change.

  • Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.
  • Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters.
  • Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.
  • Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control.
  • Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions.
Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses.

Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself.

Node.js 3rd-party Mitigation and Compensating Controls

The table below lists the rules and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-111497 and the related Node.js CVEs, ready to copy into your console.

8acca706f3c, Brotli – Request Content-EncodingCVE-2026-111497Matches inbound requests that declare Content-Encoding: br. It ships in Log mode, so set it to Block.Network (IPS)FortiGateIPS signature 62703CVE-2026-111497Blocks the crafted request inline before it reaches the decoder.Network (IPS)Check PointAdvisory CPAI-2026-15802CVE-2026-111497Blocks the exploit attempt at the gateway.Host (EDR)CrowdStrikeSuspicious Process Prevention (Linux, macOS, Windows)CVE-2026-111497, 106070, 106071, 106073Blocks a Node.js process that spawns shells, downloaders, or newly written binaries after exploitation.Host (EDR)CrowdStrikeASLR Bypass Prevention (Windows)CVE-2026-111497Blocks the ASLR bypass a reliable Brotli exploit needs. Effective only if Node.js is in the protected process set.Host (EDR)Cortex XDRCredential Gathering Protection (Linux, macOS)CVE-2026-106071, 106073Blocks unauthorized reads of credential stores, such as SSH keys and password files, that a Permission Model bypass could reach. 

Coverage is strongest for the Brotli flaw. The Cloudflare rule keys on the Content-Encoding header, so it covers requests that declare Brotli, not compressed data a service fetches or unpacks from other sources. The DNS and TLS hostname flaws depend on the interim steps above and on the upgrade.

Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation or on memory behavior, so verify each one fires for your Node.js process. Compensating controls reduce risk; upgrading Node.js remains the only complete fix.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

  1. Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.
  2. Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them.
  3. Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart.
  4. Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.
Where to Start
  1. Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths.
  2. Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality. 
  3. Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications.
  4. Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block.
  5. Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan. 

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched Node.js build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule and an IPS signature that name the Brotli flaw, with EDR watching its Node.js process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

  1. Recommendations on every finding (coming soon). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where.
  2. Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.
  3. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure.

Download the Node.js exposure dashboard today.
